utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, can we -- can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Douglas Stringer appearing on behalf of the Prosecution with Laurel Baig, Sarah Clanton and Colin Nawrot helping us here with the slides and the videos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. For Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic, lead counsel; Christopher Gosnell, co-counsel; and Toma Fila, legal consultant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. So we will start the trial with the Prosecution's opening statement. Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours, may it please the Court, Counsel. At the outset I'd like to describe three incidents from the indictment against Goran Hadzic that demonstrate the violent nature of the crimes committed in this case and their impact on victims, their families, and entire communities. On the 9th of November, 1991, Franjo Pap and his family lived in the hilly countryside outside of a town called Erdut. Erdut is situated on the western bank of the Danube River in the extreme eastern part of Croatia, a region called Eastern Slavonia. On that will day, Mr. Pap was among a group of men, ethnic Croats and Hungarians, who were arrested and taken to a military training centre in Erdut that was run by a person named Zeljko Raznjatovic better known by his nickname, Arkan. Arkan commanded a Serb military unit called the Serbian Volunteer Guard, and they were based at this training centre. Franjo Pap, together with at least 11 other prisoners arrested that day, was brutally beaten and killed at the training centre. The bodies of most of these men were put in an a mass grave in the nearby town of Celije. Franjo Pap's remains were recovered from a well located outside another town called Dalj. This incident alone wiped out the male population of several families. Franjo Pap's son, Mihajlo, was among the 12 as well as were three members of the Kalozi family, Antun, Nikola, and his son also named Nikola. Also killed were Josip, Stjepan Senasi - father and son - who by marriage were relatives of the Kalozi family. A few days later, Franjo Pap's wife, Juliana, started going around the town looking for her missing family members. She asked too many questions. She was soon arrest in Erdut along with her other son, Franjo, and a 20-year-old woman named Natalija Rakin. The three of them were executed and years later their bodies were exhumed from a well in the nearby town of Borovo Selo. The town of Ilok also sits on the Danube in eastern Croatia, south of Erdut. It was a place where about 6.700 people lived, 92 per cent of whom were Croats but ethnic Slovaks lived there as well. By mid-October 1991, the entire region where Ilok was located had been taken over by Serb armed forces who were destroying the towns and expelling its non-Serb inhabitants. Ilok was packed with those who had come from another nearby towns, Tovarnik, Bapska, Sarengrad, Lovas. The people in Ilok tried to negotiate terms with the representative of the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA, so that they could stay. But in an act that demonstrates the complete hopelessness of their situation, the people Ilok organised a referendum, a vote, on whether to leave their town altogether. The vote was held on the 13th of October, 1991. There were two questions on the referendum. Your Honours have it on the screens in front of you, or you should. The first was whether to surrender their weapons and agree to the terms demanded by the JNA. The second question on the referendum was whether to collectively move away altogether. The referendum was held on the 13th of October, 1991, and based on what they saw had happened in the neighbouring towns like Tovarnik, Sarengrad, Lovas, the people in Ilok voted against accepting the JNA's terms. They voted to leave. Some 8.000 people left Ilok in a convoy that was organised by the JNA. Four days after the referendum was held until Ilok, a group of about 100 Croat men in the nearby town of Lovas were summoned to the Zadruga building which was part of a gated complex that severed as a community centre in Lovas. The town was under the control of the Serb armed forces. The men had been summoned there before and required to perform forced labour. On this will occasion, a different form of forced labour awaited them. After they arrived on October 17th, severe beatings took place in the courtyard of the Zadruga complex. Some were singled out for special treatment, and they were stabbed and beaten with knives, metal bars, and electrical cables. On the following morning, October 18th, about 50 of the prisoners were called out by name and told to line up in pairs. The group was then marched out of the town to a clover field where mines had recently been placed. The mines had not been put there by Croatian fighters but, rather, by the Serb armed forces themselves. One of the prisoners, Bosko Bodjanac, had already been beaten so badly that he was not able to complete the march down to the clover field. He was shot on the spot and left along the side of the road. When the prisoners reached the field, they were directed at gunpoint to hold hands and walk across, sweeping their legs from side to side in order to locate and disarm the mines that had been placed there. When the first mine exploded, several Serb soldiers began firing at the prisoners in the field. And when it was over, 21 of the Croat men had been killed with more injured. The dead were buried in a mass grave at Lovas. Your Honours, this is the last opening statement of the last trial to be held in this Tribunal, but the crimes you'll hear about, such as those I've just described, were among the very first to be committed during the long years of conflict and despair that witnessed the death of a culturally rich and diverse country called Yugoslavia. In October and November of 1991, when these crimes I've just described were committed, Goran Hadzic was the leader of the government of what was called the Serbian Autonomous District of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem, what we'll call the SAO SBWS. It was Hadzic who had provided the training facility to Arkan where the Pap, Kalozi and Senasi men and many other victims in this case were beaten and killed. Hadzic's government offices were in the same compound as Arkan's training centre. On Ilok, Hadzic was involved in the talks held there between the local population and the JNA before the referendum on leaving was held, and, after the town was empty, Goran Hadzic participated in discussions to repopulate Ilok with Serbs from other places. News of the massacre in the Lovas minefield on 18 October 1991 soon became widely known and documented across the SBWS and beyond, and Hadzic was certainly aware of it. He was in Lovas for a meeting shortly after the incident occurred. Hadzic did nothing about this incident or the many other crimes he knew were taking place. He did nothing to protect the non-Serbs who lived in this region of SAO SBWS. He approved the crimes. The crimes of violence and expulsion that the thousands of victims in this case suffered were committed to further a goal shared by the accused Goran Hadzic and others the Chamber will hear about to create new territories inside Croatia that would be organised solely along ethnic lines. Your Honours, as we've learned from years of prosecuting and judging the many cases that have been preceded this one in this Tribunal, the creation of ethnically pure territories in regions that have for generations been ethnically mixed is accomplished through conflict, persecution, and violence: What we now generically call ethnic cleansing, a term that was not yet a part of our nomenclature when the first waves of crime and expulsion drove thousands from their homes and villages throughout eastern Croatia in 1991. The term "ethnic cleansing" is now of course tragically linked to the collapse of Yugoslavia itself in the 1990s, as ethnic cleansing to create territories along ethnic lines spread from Croatia to other places that are now well known to this Tribunal and the world: Sarajevo, Prijedor, Mostar, Srebrenica, Kosovo, just to name a few. But even if it didn't yet have a name at the time, what we call ethnic cleansing in the former Yugoslavia began here in Croatia in late summer and autumn of 1991, in places that are not so well known, places like Erdut, Ilok, and Lovas. The evidence will show that in the pursuit of his ambition to establish an ethnic Serbian state on the territory of Croatia, Goran Hadzic presided over a breathtakingly vicious campaign of persecution, murder, extermination, deportation forcible transfer, destruction and plunder that was directed against thousands of innocents whose sole crime was to find themselves as non-Serbs living inside the areas controlled by Hadzic and the Serb forces that supported him. The evidence will show that the crimes were all accepted and employed as part of the joint criminal enterprise that serves as a basis for Goran Hadzic's individual criminal responsibility in this case. I'll speak about the JCE, its membership, and how Hadzic contributed to it shortly. The evidence will show that Goran Hadzic is also responsible for these crimes based on his role in planning, ordering, and instigating them. He aided and abetted the others who were committing these crimes. For many of the crimes, Hadzic had the ability to prevent them from happening or to bring about investigations and prosecutions of the perpetrators. Hadzic did not use his powers or influence to prevent crimes or bring perpetrators to justice or even to speak out against what was happening. Given his high positions in the Croatian Serb leadership, his acquiescence and acceptance of crimes was itself a form of encouragement. Your Honours, in the next few sections of my submissions, I will describe a series of important political developments that provide the context for the conflict and crimes that would be taking place by August of 1991. I will then describe some of the Serb military units that figure prominently among those that committed the crimes in Croatia during the conflict. And then, before addressing the conflict and the crimes themselves, I will identify several of the members of the joint criminal enterprise and their links to Hadzic and the Serb forces that perpetrated the crimes charged in this case. The widespread lawlessness and brutality that the Chamber will hear about in this case occurred in the context of profound political change that took place in the former Yugoslavia during 1990 and 1991. I would like to mention some of these developments now, those which bear directly on the case, and, in particular, which led to the emergence of Goran Hadzic as the political leader of Serbs in Croatia during 1991 to 1993. As Your Honours know, in 1990, Croatia was one of six republics of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the SFRY which had been governed by a single party, the Communist Party, since World War II. In 1990, the Communist system gave way as individual republics held multi-party elections. The first of these multi-party elections were held in April and May of 1990 in Croatia and Slovenia. In Croatia, the Croatian Democratic Union, the HDZ, won more than 41 per cent of the vote which gave it a majority in the Croatian parliament. At the end of May 1990, that parliament elected Franjo Tudjman to be the president of the Presidency of what was still at the time the Socialist Republic of Croatia, a part of the SFRY. These events caused unease among ethnic Serbs living in Croatia. Although present in various parts of Croatia in significant numbers, the Croatian Serbs comprised about 12 per cent of the total population of Croatia compared to about 78 per cent of Croats. The remaining members of the population consisted of other ethnic groups. Croatian Serbs were concerned that in this new post-Communist Croatia they could be subject to discrimination or lose political rights that they had enjoyed under the Yugoslav system. During the latter half of 1990, the Socialist Republic of Croatia embarked on a path intended to secure its independence from Yugoslavia altogether. On the 22nd of December, 1990, the Croatian parliament promulgated a new constitution for the Republic of Croatia. Your Honours, I should add we've -- all the timeline, the dates that you're seeing should have been compiled onto a single sheet of paper which you should have, and if you don't have it, we can make sure that you do, but there is a time frame that we can -- it's in the court binder I'm informed. On the 22nd of December, 1990, the Croatian parliament promulgated a new constitution for the Republic of Croatia. Under the SFRY Constitution, Croats, Serbs, Muslims were among the six constituent nations or peoples of Yugoslavia. The Croatian Constitution of December 1990 changed that to define Croatia the national state of the Croat nation and as the state of members of other nations and minorities. Serbs and other ethnic groups were guaranteed equality with citizens of Croat nationality, but in the eyes of some Croatian Serbs, the language of the new constitution demoted them from their previous status as a constituent people to a national minority. On the 21st of February, 1991, Croatia's parliament passed a resolution initiating its disassociation from the SFRY. And on the 19th of May, 1991, a referendum was held in Croatia on independence, and a little over one month later, on the 25th of June, 1991, Croatia officially declared its independence from the SFRY. The Croatian Serbs did not remain idle during this period of profound change in Croatia and Yugoslavia. Going back to the spring of 1990, Goran Hadzic was at that time living in the town of Pacetin, located in Vukovar municipality in eastern Croatia, working as a warehouseman. Your Honours, this map shows entire -- the entirety of Croatia, and the box that you see in the upper right-hand corner is around the area that's of primary interest to us in this case, certainly during the period of 1991. And then the next map actually shows that area that was within the box we've just seen. Your Honour, I'm going to take the mouse here and try to point to a couple of the areas. I don't know if you'll be able to see them or not. I hope you do. I've mentioned Vukovar, and Vukovar is the town here, located on the Danube River, which in fact forms the boundary between Croatia here and Serbia here. This is the town of Vukovar, and Mr. Hadzic was from this region. The region -- I've mentioned the SBWS, Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem, and this map indicates each of those areas. The Vukovar area is, in general terms here, known as Slavonia or more correctly Eastern Slavonia because as we'll hear there's also a different region to the west that's called Western Slavonia. To the north is the region here called Baranja, and to the south is the region called Srijem, or Srem. And these are the three regions, if you will, that form the SAO SBWS that we'll be discussing in this case. I should mention also Srem is an ancient administrative unit that is now divided into Western Srem, which is the part in Croatia, and then the eastern part which is now in Serbia, and we'll talk later about Sremska Mitrovica, but that -- the reference there to Srem is an indication that this part of Serbia was at one time known as Eastern Srem. In the multi-party elections held in the spring of 1990, Hadzic won a seat on the Vukovar Municipal Assembly running as a member of the SDP party or the democratic -- Party for Democratic Change. However, he soon abandoned the SDP and became active in establishing a different party, the Serbian Democratic Party, or SDS, for the Vukovar region, and that was formed on the 10th of June, 1990. On that day, Mr. Hadzic was elected president of the Municipal Committee for the SDS in Vukovar. Over time, he became active in the SDS leadership for Croatia. While Hadzic and the Serbs in the Vukovar region of Eastern Slavonia were organising themselves, important developments were taking place among Serbs located in the Knin Krajina region to the west and south. This is important because the developments in the Knin Krajina were to serve as a precursor and model for the Hadzic-led move for Serb autonomy in his own region of Eastern Slavonia. Later, the different Serb autonomous areas or districts served as the genesis for what's called the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, the RSK, which Hadzic would become president of in 1992. Your Honours, this map indicates the area generally of what was to become the SAO Krajina, with the blue borders being an indication of what was the territory declared, and then this will be evidence of one of the upcoming witnesses, the red generally referring to the areas that were under Serb control. So the areas as declared did not totally match with the areas that fell under military control and essentially the red would indicate the area of confrontation lines. This is the SAO Krajina here, and we'll talk more about this area throughout these submissions. The Knin Krajina Serbs were led by Milan Babic, who on the 31st of July, 1990, became the president of a body called the Serbian National Council, SNC, and this was to operate as the executive branch of a Serbian Assembly which had been established in the Knin region one week earlier. This Assembly had declared sovereignty and autonomy of the Serb people in Croatia one week earlier on the 25th of July, 1990. The Knin Krajina SAO declared itself as a sovereign autonomous region in Croatia. Within about five weeks' time, by the 2nd of September, 1990, the SNC had called for and held a referendum for Serbs on autonomy of Serbs inside Croatia, and the Serbs voted overwhelmingly in favour of autonomy, about 97 per cent in favour. On the 21st of December, 1990, the Knin Municipal Assembly adopted a decision establishing what was called the autonomous Serbian district, or SAO for Krajina. This decision provided that the institutions of the SAO Krajina would be responsible for the district's proper functioning and that it, the SAO Krajina, would implement the laws of Croatia within that territory. One day after the decision declaring the SAO Krajina, on the 22nd of December, 1990, as I've already mentioned, the Croatian parliament promulgated the new constitution. Under Milan Babic, the SAO Krajina moved rapidly to establish complete autonomy within Croatia. Separate parallel institutions such as the police were set up to replace the same Croatian institutions. On the 5th of January, 1991, the Executive Council of the SAO Krajina revoked the authority of the Croatian Ministry of Internal Affairs, the MUP, or the police, to operate inside its territory. All remaining links with Croatia were severed on the 1st of April, 1991. When the SAO Krajina Executive Council voted to secede from Croatia. It issued a decision on accession of the SAO Krajina to the Republic of Serbia. In early 1991, Hadzic and the Serbs in the region of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem began taking similar steps to establish their own separate parallel Serb structures, and ultimately a wholly autonomous Serb territory there. A few moments ago I mentioned the Serbs of the Knin Krajina had formed a Serb National Council, or SNC, on the 31st of July, 1990, that served as an executive body for a Serb Assembly. On the 7th of January, 1991, a group of Serbs including Goran Hadzic formed the same body, the SNC, for the SBWS region. A separate Serb police force was later established in Borovo Selo, a town we'll see on the map soon. This was a majority Serb town located about 10 kilometres north of Vukovar. Goran Hadzic appointed a Serb to be in charge of the new Serb police force in Borovo Selo. The creation of separate Serb and Croat police and security forces both in the Knin region and the Vukovar area is an extremely important development. As we will see, the first armed conflicts that occurred in the war between the Serbs and the Croats in Croatia involved police units. Second, the evidence will show that these newly created Serb police and security units were financed and equipped by the Republic of Serbia. On the 26th of February, 1991, the SBWS Serb National Council, the SNC executive body, issued a declaration on the sovereign autonomy of the Serb Nation of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem. This provided that the Serb people in that area would exercise sovereign autonomy through supreme legislative and executive power in relation to specified issues of autonomy, including the protection of peace and security. The SBWS government structures came into being on the 25th of June, 1991. This is a day of tremendous importance. As we've already noted, it was on this day that the Croatian parliament declared Croatia to be independent from Yugoslavia. International recognition of Croatia was not to come for another six months, but the lack of official recognition from outside does not appear to have had any effect on the events that were now taking place inside Croatia. On the same day that Croatia declared its independence from Yugoslavia, Serbs from the region of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem met at a place called Backa Palanka located on the Serbian side of the Danube River not far from Vukovar. There the Serbs of the SBWS voted to secede from Croatia. They created a legislative body called the Grand or the Great National Assembly which then issued a decision on the position of the person people from SBWS essentially declaring that the Serbs in that territory had decided to remain within a single country along with the other parts populated by Serbs and other Yugoslav nations which want to live in a united Yugoslav state. It declared that the Yugoslav constitution would continue to apply in this territory. Also, Your Honours, it was on the 25th of June, 1991, that Goran Hadzic was designated to be the president of the government of the SBWS, its prime minister, if you will, or chief executive. Goran Hadzic was officially appointed to that position, president of the government, three months later on the 25th of September, 1991. But the evidence will show that, as Prime Minister-designate, Hadzic exercised his authority well in advance of his formal appointment on the 25th of September. Your Honours, this slide is Article 4 -- shows Article 4 of the 25th of June, 1991, decision on the position of the Serb people of the SBWS that I just referred to: "Citizens who live on the territory of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem are equal in their rights and duties and they have the same protection before state and other bodies, regardless of their race, language, sex, nationality, religion ...," et cetera. Your Honours, the evidence is going to show that this was absolutely tragically not true. Within a few short months after the adoption of this declaration, certain citizens found that they not only had no protection before official bodies of the SBWS but that they, in fact, were the target of this so-called state of SBWS. It soon became open season in Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem on anyone who wasn't a Serb. Croats, Hungarians, Slovaks who lived in the region were targeted for persecution, violence, forcible eviction, and were murdered in large numbers as the SBWS was cleansed of its non-Serb population. Even Serbs who protested against the persecution of their non-Serb neighbours were driven out. The evidence will show that in the months and years that followed the 25th of June, 1991, Goran Hadzic used his positions of leadership in the Serb-held territories of Croatia to facilitate and encourage the violent persecution and forcible transfer -- forcible removal of Croats and other non-Serbs from the SBWS territory. This was a goal that he shared with others in the joint criminal enterprise that is charged in the indictment. Your Honours, coming back now to this map. This shows the locations of the SAO Krajina, as I previously mentioned, and now the location of the SBWS SAO, again with the blue being the are declared, red being, the evidence will show, the area actually held. A third SAO, which I have not yet mentioned is the SAO Western Slavonia, which was declared in August of 1991. That's in this area. In the middle of the northern section of Croatia. Goran Hadzic did not play a significant role in establishing the SAO Western Slavonia, but Your Honours will hear evidence regarding relevant events and developments that took place there during the latter part of 1991 and after. These three SAOs existed separately in Croatia for only a fairly short period. On December 19th of 1991, the SAO Krajina, which was -- which just nine months earlier had voted to secede from Croatia, purporting to join Serbia, now declared itself to be a fully independent state, the Republic of the Serbian Krajina or RSK. On the 26th of February, 1992, the other two SAOs that we've seen, SBWS and Western Slavonia, joined the RSK, and on the same day, 26th of February, 1992, Goran Hadzic became the president of the republic, the president of the RSK. He would remain in that position to the end of 1993. The establishment of the three SAOs by the summer of 1991 claimed territory in Croatia that was to be autonomous Serb territory. But at that time, not everyone shared the same vision of what life would be like inside the SAOs for the people, Serbs and non-Serbs alike, who lived there. The evidence will show that for some, the establishment of SAOs was an attempt to preserve Serbian identity, culture, language, such as the Cyrillic script, within the framework of a new Croatia. For others, however, the vision was much different, much more extreme. They saw the SAOs as largely mono-ethnic territories for which there would be no place for non-Serbs. In order to achieve this vision, populations would have to move. People would have to be driven out, others brought in. Ultimately, this was the vision that prevailed. This brings us to the common criminal purpose of the joint criminal enterprise charged in this case. Your Honours, the evidence will show that a group of people among whom is this accused, Goran Hadzic, intended to make the SAOs in Croatia as mono-ethnic - as Serbian - as possible. They knew and accepted that to achieve this goal, the non-Serb populations would have to be removed and that this could only be done by force and by making life so difficult and miserable for those not yet forcibly removed that they would have no choice but to leave. The evidence will show that for Goran Hadzic, the focus was on securing the removal of the non-Serb population from the territory of the SAO SBWS during roughly the months of August through December 1991. Hadzic continued to contribute to this goal throughout the combined territory now of the RSK as its president during 1992 and 1993. Through his high-level positions in the Croatian Serb leadership and through his close association with the leadership of the Republic of Serbia, Hadzic made multiple contributions to the JCE. I'd like to identify a few of those now. I'll return to this in greater detail later as we discuss specific events after the conflict began. First, Hadzic was a formulator and implementing of discriminatory policies. Goran Hadzic established and led government bodies which formulated and implemented policies that discriminated against non-Serbs, ensuring that they would -- they were expelled from the area and would not return. Discriminatory measures enacted by the governments under Hadzic's authority included the appropriation of Croatian state assets as well as "abandoned" private property, that is property left behind by the people who no longer live there, enabling his government to seize the property of non-Serbs. Under his authority, the RSK enacted legislation permitting the resettlement of only those people who had a clean war record and had not collaborated with the "enemy." Legislation intended to restore the pre-World War II ethnic composition of certain areas was also passed in order to promote the return of Serbs who had left these areas during the World War II area. There was also a decision banning all Croatian citizens from entering the RSK. These measures were discriminatory and were intended to ensure non-Serbs would leave and that those who had already left or been expelled would not return. Hadzic was a co-ordinator. Using his position of authority, Goran Hadzic contributed and facilitated the work of the local Serbs and militias with that of military units arriving from Serbia and ensured that his government ministers did so as well. I will talk about the various Serb forces that committed the many crimes charged in this case. Goran Hadzic was the civilian leader of the SBWS government, and later the RSK, and in those capacities, he served as an important connection between civilian authority and the various Serb armed forces. He was fully engaged in military discussions, planning and operations. As I'll mention later, the evidence will show that certain Serb forces or units and their military commanders were integrated within Hadzic's civilian government. Goran Hadzic was a supplier. The evidence will show that Hadzic contributed to the JCE by using his position of authority to ensure that the Serb forces operating in Croatia had the resources, materials, and weapons they needed to take control over the territory they claimed for the SAO SBWS. For materials, weapons, and money, the SBWS was completely dependent on Serbia and the continued support of its leadership. The evidence will show that Goran Hadzic was frequently in Belgrade meeting with Serbian leaders and working to procure weapons for the Serb forces operating in the SBWS. The few assets available locally, whether privately owned or former property of the Croatian republic, those were also appointed and used to the same end. Hadzic was an implementer of Serbian policy. Hadzic's trips to Belgrade weren't just about obtaining money and weapons. He also went there to receive instructions and guidance and to consult with key figures in Serbia's leadership who not only shared his goal of creating ethnic Serb territory in Croatia by violence, but also who had the money and the power to make it happen. Hadzic needed them precisely because they had the money, power, and know-how to make the plan a reality. They needed Hadzic because he was a Serb from Croatia whom they could influence or control to ensure that their policies in Croatia would be implemented. First, in the SAO SBWS, and then in the RSK, Goran Hadzic was Slobodan Milosevic's man on the ground in Croatia. President Milosevic and the Serb leadership needed Hadzic not only to implement their policies on the ground in Croatia, but also to ensure that their policies and decisions would be carried out in dealings with the international community. From the very earliest days of the conflict, Hadzic was the face of the SAO SBWS, and later the RSK, in international meetings and negotiations concerning the conflict in Croatia. The evidence will show that as early as September 1991, Goran Hadzic was involved in negotiations with the EU which was trying to broker a cease-fire. The Dutch ambassador to France, Henry Wynaendts, led negotiations and met with Hadzic in the town of Borovo Selo. After consulting with Slobodan Milosevic, Hadzic signed the cease-fire agreement on behalf of Croatian Serbs. That's an agreed fact, Your Honours. The following month, October 1991, Hadzic travelled here to The Hague for more talks, and the Trial Chamber will have evidence of that. We'd now like to put up a short video-clip from early 1993. This is taken just shortly before Goran Hadzic flew out to New York for talks there on the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. Here he expresses the view that the only solution is for there to be a border between the Serbian and Croatian people. In this footage, Mr. Hadzic is accompanied by Mile Paspalj, who at the time was president of the RSK Assembly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Journalist: What are your expectations regarding the dialogue in New York in the upcoming days? "Goran Hadzic: I expect a constructive dialogue but I also expect we will be put under some pressure. We are prepared for that and we are also ready to tell to the co-chairman and to the whole world the truth about the Serbian people and the only possible solution and that is the border between the Serbia and the Croatian people which would secure a lasting peace in this area."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will have evidence of many meetings and negotiations that Hadzic had with members of the international community from 1991 through 1993. Hadzic's recognised role on the international stage undoubtedly gave him tremendous influence and provided him with a real opportunity to contribute to the restoration of order and the prevention of ethnic-based crimes. The evidence will show that during the course of his many meetings and negotiations with members of the international community, Hadzic was repeatedly confronted with the allegations and evidence of ethnic cleansing and expulsion of non-Serbs. He did not use his influence to stop these crimes or even attempt to do so. The evidence will show that Goran Hadzic had no regard for the plight of non-Serbs living within the Serb-controlled areas under his authority. Hadzic was a direct participant in crimes. Goran Hadzic was not merely a bystander observing or turning a blind eye to the crimes occurring around him. The evidence will show that he directly participated in and facilitated crimes against non-Serbs. Together with other JCE members, he planned the mass expulsion of non-Serbs from the area under his authority to Croat-controlled territory. He personally ordered the unlawful detention of non-Serbs and released detainees into Arkan's custody. As I will discuss in further detail, following the fall of Vukovar, he personally ensured that at least 200 Croat prisoners remained in the SBWS and were not moved out to Serbia, and shortly, I will describe what happened to those prisoners. Hadzic was a fueler of persecutory environment and a creator of an environment of impunity. Finally, throughout the indictment period, Goran Hadzic repeatedly and publicly proclaimed that Serbs and Croats could not live together, fuelling the persecutory and coercive atmosphere that encouraged or forced non-Serbs to flee. He remained mute in the face of certain knowledge of persistent, ethnic-based crimes that was occurring on his doorstep, creating an environment in which those committing the crimes in the area under his authority knew that they could do so with impunity and were encouraged to commit more crimes. The evidence will show that by all his acts and his omissions, Goran Hadzic contributed to the criminal purpose which he shared with his fellow JCE members. That purpose was the violent removal of non-Serbs from the areas of Croatia perceived to be Serb territory. Now a few words about the Serb forces that I've been referring to. The evidence will show that the dirty work was done by a number of different military units and organisations. Some of these were local units, others came from Serbia. Sometimes these units worked separately, other times they worked together. But at all times the Serb forces, as they're defined in paragraph 11 of the indictment, were fulfilling the task of riding the SAO of its non-Serb population. I'd like to briefly describe here just a few of the non-Serb -- of the Serb forces that the Chamber will have evidence about in this case. After that, I'll talk more about the individuals, other members of the JCE who are most closely associated with these Serb forces. The Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA, was at the outset the army for all of Yugoslavia. That was its constitutional role. As Yugoslavia began to fall apart, however, the JNA's role changed. The evidence will show that after the Serbs in Croatia declared their independence, the JNA was gradually transformed. By mid-1991, the evidence will show that the JNA was essentially a Serb army whose mission was to protect Serbs outside Serbia. The evidence will show that for the JNA, the protection of Serbs in Croatia meant intervening militarily to remove Croatian institutions, authorities, and armed forces from Serb majority areas, but it soon went beyond that. The evidence will show that the JNA was among those Serb forces that directly participated in the cleansing of large numbers of non-Serb civilians all across the SBWS, including areas where Croats, not Serbs, were far and away the largest ethnic group. The role played by the JNA in Ilok, which we mentioned at the beginning of our submissions, this is an example of this. The transformation of the JNA from a Yugoslav People's Army to a Serb army involved in ethnic cleansing of non-Serbs in Croatia was carried out by JCE members who were in the JNA and Serbian leadership such as Generals Kadijevic and Adzic, and with the support of Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic. The Serbian Volunteer Guard, SDG, was led by Arkan, Zeljko Raznjatovic. The SDG were also called the Arkanovci, Arkan's Men, or Arkan's Tigers. Arkan and the SDG were sent to Dalj in the SBWS by Jovica Stanisic, who was chief of the Serbian State Security Department or the DB. Serbia's state security and Ministry of Defence continued to sponsor this unit, the SDG, ensuring that it was well equipped with weapons and ammunition. By August of 1991, Arkan's Men were installed at the training centre facility in Erdut made available to them by Goran Hadzic. This was the training centre where the men of the Pap, Kalozi, and Senasi families were taken in November 1991, beaten and killed. The training centre was within the same gated compound as the seat and offices of Goran Hadzic's SBWS government. After 1991, Arkan's Men moved to the Knin Krajina region of the RSK, and they fought there in 1992, before moving south to participate in the conflict after it spread to Bosnia-Herzegovina. The evidence will show that local Serbs within the SAOs in Croatia organised themselves into militias, or Territorial Defence forces, that participated in the expulsion of non-Serbs from the areas that they controlled. In this they worked in tandem with units from the JNA that were not from the area, and they participated in many crimes and expulsions. The commander of the local Territorial Defence for the SBWS was not a local. Radovan Stojicic, shown as Badza, was sent from Serbia to take command of the SBWS TO, Territorial Defence. Later, when Hadzic was president of the RSK, RSK units of Territorial Defence were transformed into Special Police Units, and these RSK police units played a key role in crimes committed during 1992 and 1993. The Serbian National Security, or SNB, was a Special Police Unit that provided personal security for Goran Hadzic and his SBWS government. The evidence will show that the members of the SNB committed numerous crimes and killings of non-Serbs in the SBWS, and they frequently collaborated with Arkan and his men in this. Serb forces that were active and committing crimes in the SBWS in 1991 also included many volunteers who were sent from Serbia. Several nationalist political parties in Serbia formed volunteer units and dispatched them to Croatia. Among these, Vojislav Seselj organised his own volunteers, commonly referred to as Chetniks or Seselj's Men. Seselj, who is here at this Tribunal awaiting the judgement in his own case, was the leader of the Serbian Chetnik Movement and the Serbian Radical Party, the SRS. Seselj held extremist views on ethnic separation and restoration of a Greater Serbia that would encompass substantial parts of Croatia as well as Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Serbian Ministry of Defence - excuse me - was heavily involved in the organisation of volunteers and in their training, equipping, arming for deployment to Croatia. The JNA incorporated volunteers from Serbia in its operations in Croatia. The Red Berets were a special unit that was formed, financed, equipped and deployed by the Serbian state security, the DB. This unit also participated in crimes against non-Serbs. This unit was known also as Frenki's men for its commander, JCE member Franko Simatovic. This unit had bases in Tikves and Ilok and was active in the SBWS and in other parts of Croatia. This unit participated in the takeover of Vukovar and killed five non-Serbs in Grabovac, which is one of the incidents in this indictment charged in paragraph 37. Your Honours, here I'd like to speak about a few of the more prominent JCE members that are charged in the indictment as being part of the common criminal purpose with Goran Hadzic. Slobodan Milosevic was the president of the Republic of Serbia and the most powerful figure in the JCE. During the relevant times in this case, Milosevic controlled all major decisions and institutions of the Serbian government. Through his position, he was able to exercise control over and influence Serbian forces such as its MUP and the JNA. This made him in all likelihood the most powerful person in the former Yugoslavia during the indictment period, 1990 to 1993. His dominance was built on manipulation of Serbian nationalist policies, the essence of which was that Serbs must live in a territory controlled by Serbs. He surrounded himself with loyal supports. Hadzic and other JCE members rallied around Milosevic and shared his nationalistic sentiments of Serbian unity and ethnic separation. Jovica Stanisic was the chief of the State Security Department, the SDB, for the Republic of Serbia. This was a part of the Serbian MUP, Ministry of Internal Affairs. He was formally appointed to this position in December of 1991, but he exercised de facto authority over the DB in the months preceding his formal appointment. Franko Simatovic, also known as Frenki, was his deputy. As Your Honours know, the trial of Messrs. Stanisic and Simatovic in this Tribunal is in its final stages. Stanisic and Simatovic controlled and co-ordinated the arming, training and deployment of volunteer formations in the SBWS, SAO Krajina, and later in the RSK. Arkan's Tigers and the Red Berets were among these. In my first remarks, I mentioned the people of Ilok who'd voted to leave rather than stay and the involvement of Goran Hadzic in discussions about resettling Serbs there. The discussions were held in Stanisic's hometown of Backa Palanka, which is located on the other side of the Danube River, directly opposite Ilok. Jovica Stanisic was present with Hadzic when this was discussed in late October or early November of 1991. Mihalj Kertes was another Belgrade-based member of the JCE. He was a member of the Serbian Presidency in 1989 and 1990 and was president -- sorry, deputy federal minister for foreign affairs in Serbia in 1992. The evidence will show that Kertes provided weapons, logistical and financial support to Serbian police and paramilitary units that were operating in Croatia. His sphere of responsibility involved looking after the interests of Serbs outside Serbia, especially in Slavonia and in the Krajinas. Kertes was closely associated with Stanisic, Simatovic, and Milosevic. I've mentioned Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan. He was the commander of the Serbian Volunteer Guard, also known as Arkan's Tigers. The evidence will show that Arkan was dispatched to the SBWS by Jovica Stanisic, who, as I mentioned, was the head of Serbia's DB, state security. Arkan is one of the core JCE members with whom Goran Hadzic collaborated in this case. Arkan was a known criminal even before 1991, and is a notorious perpetrator of crimes committed in this case. By August of 1991, SBWS Prime Minister-designate Goran Hadzic had installed the SAO SBWS government at a winery facility in Erdut. Inside the compound was Arkan's training centre, which I've already referred to. Many prisoners were brought to the training centre for interrogations and beatings before being killed. As indicated here, when the conflict spread to Bosnia from Croatia, Arkan and his unit fought in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was indicted by this Tribunal, but he was never tried. He was assassinated in Belgrade in January of 2000. Arkan and his men also participated in joint actions with the JNA authority the SBWS. JNA General Andrija Biorcevic was commander of the 12th JNA Novi Sad Corps in November of 1991, and that unit directly participated in the JNA's operations, was a part of the JNA's operations in the SBWS. We're going to play a short video-clip that was taken in 1992 in which Biorcevic is speaking. And after referring to the destruction of Vukovar, which we'll be getting to shortly, Biorcevic praised Arkan and the tactics they employed together in their joint operations.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] And of our own initiative, we did what we did, but we would not have destroyed it to the extent that we did had they decided to surrender, but they didn't want to surrender; and, secondly: The men did not want to charge, you know. You can go about attacking, using equipment to no end, but if you don't have a man who will seize it ... that's the greatest merit of Arkan's volunteers. Some are imputing, however, that I am acting in collusion with paramilitary formations. Those are not paramilitary formations here. Those are men who have come voluntarily to fight for the Serb people; we encircle a village, he storms in, and whoever doesn't want to surrender - he kills off and we move on."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the other gentleman shown in the video on the other side of the woman is Arkan. We'll have more images of him soon. In this video, General Biorcevic describes the general role of the JNA during its operations in the SBWS. With its superior military capability, the JNA would first attack and break the defence of the targeted town or village or surround it. It would then step back while units such as Arkan's Men, local TOs or volunteers stepped in to do the mopping up. This alone tells us much about how different Serb forces worked together. But Arkan did not just kill enemy soldiers who refused to surrender. In this video an interview that Arkan gave in English in late 1991, probably in September, to French television, Arkan describes his policy on the treatment of prisoners generally.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Reporter: Don't be shy. "Zeljko Raznjatovic: We don't take any more prisoners. We're gonna kill every fascist soldier we catch. They have to know that. No prisoners because they took two prisoners, our prisoners. This is a 19-years, 19-years-old soldier who was captured by the fascist Croatian Army - the Ustashi. And he was tortured till death. We can't forget about past when 33 members of my family were killed in the Second World War, tortured like my soldier was tortured; like this."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The evidence will show that when Arkan -- what Arkan said, when he said that he doesn't take prisoners, it wasn't just soldierly bravado for the camera here. He was telling the truth. And this is not just limited to Croat soldiers. Arkan did not distinguish between soldiers, prisoners, or civilians. They were all treated the same. The only distinction he made was between Serbs and non-Serbs. In next slide is from a JNA report about Arkan's training programme. This is a report from the 25th of October, 1991: "Through the training process of each volunteer, they learn, when raiding into a Croatian house, to kill whom they find in the house, no matter if those are children, old and frail people, women and similar. They train them to open fire from left to right when engaged in the killings." The evidence will show that after Arkan arrived in Erdut in August of 1991, he became a close associate of Goran Hadzic. They were frequently together. This is a still photograph taken from a video from the early part of November 1991, at the funeral of General Mladen Bratic. He had been the commander of the JNA Novi Sad Corps. He was killed in combat operations near Vukovar. The incident charged in paragraph 24 of the indictment is an example of the close collaboration, the criminal collaboration, between Hadzic and Arkan. The evidence will show that on the 21st of September, 1991, Hadzic and Arkan together, accompanied by 12 [sic] of Arkan's men, went to the Dalj police station where a group of prisoners was being held. Hadzic had ordered that these prisoners be brought to the police headquarters about one week earlier on the pretense they were to stand trial. Hadzic and Arkan released two of the men. Eleven others were taken away by Arkan. We know his policy on prisoners. They were executed. And in 1998, the remains of nine of those 11 were exhumed from the village of Celije and from a well in Dalj. Another member of the joint criminal enterprise in this case is Radovan Stojicic, also known as Badza. Like Arkan, he was not a local but, rather, was from Serbia, where he was a high-level official of the Serbian MUP or Interior Ministry. He arrived in Erdut around August 1991 and took command of the local TO, Territorial Defence units. The evidence will show that Stojicic was in regular contact with Hadzic and Arkan. Also, Stojicic was in frequent virtually daily contact with the command of the JNA Novi Sad Corps, and he co-ordinated joint actions of the JNA with the TO units that he commanded. Also, Stojicic, Badza, attended certain meetings of the SAO SBWS government, and he briefed its members on the military situation on the ground. Milan Martic was a police officer from Knin who severed as its chief of police. During 1991, he was appointed to various high positions in the SAO Krajina such as secretary of internal affairs, minister of defence, minister of interior. In August of that year, 1991, he was also named deputy commander of the TO, the SAO Krajina. After the SAO SBWS and Western Slavonia joined the RSK in February of 1992, Martic served as the minister of interior while Goran Hadzic was RSK president. Martic was in charge of the police which included not only regular police units but also heavily armed Special Police militias that were involved in many crimes committed against non-Serbs during 1992 and 1993. In 1994, Mr. Martic became president of the RSK. Based in part on his role in crimes committed against non-Serbs in the SAO Krajina and RSK, Milan Martic was indicted by this Tribunal in 2003. In 2008, he was convicted and sentenced to 35 years' imprisonment. Although he's not identified as a JCE member in the indictment, I would like to mention Stevo Bogic, as known as Jajo. Bogic was a Serb from Vukovar appointed by Goran Hadzic to head a unit called the Serbian National Security, the SNB. The SNB is among the Serbs forces that are identified in paragraph 11 of the indictment. The SNB was a Special Police Unit that provided personal security for Goran Hadzic and his SBWS government. Stevo Bogic's office was located in the centre at the Erdut Winery complex some 10 metres away from Goran Hadzic's office. He reported directly to Hadzic. The evidence will show that members of the SNB committed numerous crimes and killings of non-Serbs in the SBWS, and they frequently collaborated with Arkan and his men. Bogic provided Arkan's men with SNB identification cards to ensure their free movement in the area. Bogic was also a minister in the SBWS government and later was a minister in the RSK government. Your Honours, I would note here that with Arkan and his training centre -- with Arkan and his training centre based in the same physical location as Hadzic's SBWS government, with Stevo Bogic of the SNB working just down the hall, and with Radovan Stojicic briefing Hadzic's SBWS government on the actions of the various JNA and TO formations, Hadzic had ensured that civilian government structures of the SBWS would be well integrated with the military structures operating there. Your Honours, we've now described the establishment of the SAOs, the Serbian autonomous districts or regions in Croatia, the common criminal purpose of the JCE and Hadzic's contribution to it, as well as some of the more prominent Serb forces and JCE members. I would now like to address the armed conflict and the various crimes about which the Trial Chamber will hear during the trial. First, I would like to mention the beginning of the armed conflict. Your Honours, the evidence will show that the armed conflict began during the period of late March to early May 1991, when units of the newly created Serb MUP or police clashed with their counterparts on the Croatian side. A significant conflict took place on the 31st of March, 1991, at a place called Plitvice in Central Croatia. And here Your Honours see a map of Croatia with the location of the Plitvice National Park indicated. Hundreds of armed Croatian MUP personnel were brought into the area in late March of 1991 to restore Croatian control there. That's because the park was in - excuse me - within the territory of what had been declared to be the SAO Krajina. The Croatian MUP personnel there encountered armed police units of the SAO Krajina. The JNA was also present and intervened. A cease-fire was agreed. Several police personnel were wounded in the incident. The evidence will show that at the time of the incident at Plitvice, Goran Hadzic was one of the SDS leaders for the areas of Knin and Vukovar. He and other members of the SDS leadership had come for a conference in Benkovac to the south. While travelling back to the Vukovar area, Hadzic and another Serb political figure, Borivoje Savic, were arrested by the Croatian authorities and they were detained. Hadzic was beaten and mistreated while he was in the custody of the Croatian authorities. He was released after several days. There will be evidence that after his arrest and mistreatment at Plitvice, Hadzic became more extreme in his politics and in his views about relations between Serbs and Croats in Croatia. If there had been two visions for the SAOs in Croatia, preservation of Serbian culture and identity within Croatia versus complete separation and establishment of autonomous, ethnic Serb territory in Croatia, Hadzic was definitely in the latter camp after Plitvice. His orientation shifted to Belgrade, and by June of 1991, Hadzic would inform one of his more moderate colleagues in the SDS that he, Hadzic, was going to war. The evidence will show that Goran Hadzic held the view that Serbs and Croats could not co-exist. This wasn't just his personal opinion. This was to become the policy of his government. Croats were to be driven out and not permitted to return. Your Honour, I can address one more incident and then -- just another page of my outline and then it would be a good time for a break, if you're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: After Plitvice, a significant armed conflict between Croats and Serbs occurred much closer to home. I've already mentioned Borovo Selo, a Serb town located a short distance north of Vukovar. This map, Your Honours, indicates the location of Borovo Selo in Eastern Slavonia. Again, with the mouse - we've already got the arrow there - Your Honours can see Vukovar here and then the town of Borovo just to the north. Here is Dalj. Here is Erdut. By May of 1991, the Serbs in Borovo Selo, like many Serbs in many parts of Croatia at the time, had erected barricades to isolate the town and prevent Croatian personnel, such as the police, from entering. Here's a photo that gives an idea of what barricades looked like at the time. On the 2nd of May, 1991, the Croatian authorities sent five buses of Croatian police into Borovo Selo. This was in response to the arrest of two Croatian police officers the previous evening. The result was a battle between the Croat police on one side and local Serbs, together with volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party, the SRS, Seselj's people, who were also present in Borovo at the time. Twelve Croatian policemen and three Serbs were killed at Borovo Selo during that incident on the 2nd of May, and more were wounded. Your Honour, if this is a good time for a break. I see we're at about 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Prosecutor. So we will break now and come back at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You may continue, Mr. Stringer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, before the break, we described the incidents, first at Plitvice in March of 1991 and then the incident in Borovo Selo, on -- in early May of 1991, and I'd like now to move to August of 1991. The conflict continued to escalate during the summer months of 1991. During June, July, and August of that year, the JNA forces began sporadically shelling parts of Vukovar. The intensity grew as the summer went on. On the 1st of August, 1991, the town of Dalj was taken by local Serbs and the JNA which, on that day, crossed over from Serbia and deployed extensive heavy weaponry into the area. Some 50 JNA tanks were in the area of Erdut and Dalj, shelling Erdut as they moved through the area. The evidence will show that a JNA tank fired on the police station at Dalj and the building was destroyed. A number of Croat policemen were killed there. This map shows the location of the town of Dalj, a short distance north of Vukovar just below Erdut, on the Danube. And, again, the arrow indicates Dalj, with Vukovar to the south, and Erdut just to the north, all sitting along the banks of the Danube. The Chamber will have evidence that Goran Hadzic was present with the JNA at the Dalj police station on the 1st of August after the town had been taken. Once the Serb forces captured Dalj, they had a foothold inside Croatia from which they extended their military and political control throughout the territory declared by the SAO SBWS. By late August of 1991, the JNA and other Serb forces had overrun the entire district of Baranja to the north of Dalj, this area on the map that I'm indicating with the map. Even though the area overall had a relatively small Serb population of about 20 to 25 per cent. During September and October of 1991, Serb forces, principally the JNA, took towns in Western Srem to the south and east of Vukovar, such as Ilok, Sarengrad, Bapska, Lovas, and Tovarnik. And, Your Honour, this map then shows the general area of those towns. With the mouse again, I'll just indicate Ilok in the far eastern edge of Western Srem, Sarengrad, Lovas - the location of the minefield incident that was earlier described - Bapska, Tovarnik. As Your Honours can see from this map, taking control of Western Srem secured the eastern edge of the SBWS along the Danube River and effectively eliminated the Croatian border that had separated the SBWS from its sponsor state, Serbia. The pattern in taking Western Srem was to combine shelling attacks with ultimatums directed to local residents. To illustrate this, I'd like to describe what happened in the town of Bapska. By late September of 1991, as the JNA and other Serb forces took control over the Western Srem area, the residents of Bapska were, like virtually all the other Croats in the area, either fleeing or negotiating terms with the Serb forces to allow them to remain. In Bapska, the negotiations were between the president of the local commune and a JNA commander. The JNA commander issued an ultimatum directing that, although the residents of Bapska had been peaceful so far, they must nonetheless, by 1600 hours on the 28th of September, 1991, surrender any weapons they had to the JNA. This next slide, Your Honours, is from Exhibit 65 ter 0418. This is from the ultimatum that was issued on at that day. And as Your Honours will see in item 2, the JNA added this incentive to the residents of Bapska: "If this is not done by this time, you can count on your village ceasing to exist on the geographical map." Many people of Bapska fled to nearby Ilok where they met residents of the towns of Tovarnik, Lovas, and Sarengrad, who had also fled to Ilok because of the threats and the attacks of the Serb forces in their own towns. Ilok is the place I mentioned in my introductory comments. It's the place where the conditions were so bad that the people held a referendum on October 13th 1991 and decided to leave of town altogether. By emptying Ilok, the Serb forces had effectively emptied much of Western Srem of its non-Serb inhabitants. They'd been systematically pushed eastward toward Ilok, the Danube River, and the Serbian border. And now they were gone. We're now in mid-October of 1991, Your Honours. Before continuing, I'd like to focus for a moment on Goran Hadzic and the level of his own involvement and knowledge about all that's happened so far. In the first video-clip that we saw of Mr. Hadzic, he was flying to New York in early 1993 for negotiations. This video is from Erdut. He's uniformed and appears to be carrying a sidearm. He describes military developments and events taking place throughout the SBWS. His references to the liberation of Western Srem, events in Ilok and the ongoing battle for Vukovar tell us that this interview would have occurred around mid-October 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Anchor: We are moving to Slavonia and Western Srem. "Reporter: Dear viewers, following the press conference held in Erdut today, we asked Goran Hadzic, president of the Serb region of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem, to answer some questions for viewers of the Belgrade Television. "Mr. Hadzic, to what extent is fierce fighting going on, if we can put it that way, in this theatre of war? What are the prospects of this war? "Goran Hadzic: Fights are intense. This first action, first part, meaning liberation of Western Srem, is in its final stage. As I said, fights for Vukovar are ongoing. We can say that our units control nearly 50 per cent of the city. We have secure positions and are advancing house by house. The action of mopping up Ustasha villages was also carried out in the last two days. Following mopping up of Sid-Vinkovci section, couple of Ustasha villages in this section of the central part of our region were mopped up three days ago, so Bogdanovci and the villages down there. Some villages surrender. In Ilok, specifically, one wing offers to surrender while the other, extreme wing, will not allow it. I will have talks regarding this issue today, so they can surrender their weapons and perpetrators can be held responsible before law and the innocent and stay and live with us. "Reporter: This territorial army, defenders of the villages, Yugoslav People's Army, going to launch a stronger offensive since, as you yourself are aware, there is talk about great -- a great number of complaints with regard to intense war activities especially by the Yugoslav People's Army? "Goran Hadzic: Well there are complaints these are, I could say, relatively justified given the attitude and possibilities. Our primary goal is not the mass killing of Croats, but punishing criminals in their midst. This means we have tried everything through democratic and other peaceful means to prevent this. However, even after our signing the truce, agreements and negotiations, the Ustasha continue disregarding the signatures. It means that everyone with this ... I do not trust them at all. This is clear to me - there can be no negotiations with them, and the situation has to be resolved militarily. The communique of the Supreme Command speaks to this effect, but we have to be aware that the army cannot carry this out without the people. So we will have to have some co-ordinated action, a real co-ordinated action between the people and the army."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So what does this tell us? This tells us that a uniformed president of the government, Goran Hadzic, was fully informed on the JNA's cleansing of towns in Western Srem such as Tovarnik, Bapska, Lovas. He also knew that closer to home, "our units," as he calls them, were moving house to house in Vukovar and were "mopping up" Ustasha villages, as he describes them, in the region around Vukovar. As Your Honours will know, "Ustasha" is a term linked to what was called the Independent State of Croatian from World War II. This was a fascist regime that exterminated large numbers of Serbs and Jews while allied with Nazi Germany. Referring to Croats as Ustashas was guaranteed to ratchet up fear and tension among Hadzic's listens. The evidence will show that Goran Hadzic frequently used the term Ustasha as a way of referring to all Croats as here in referring to "Ustasha villages." This not only contributed to fear and division but also served to demonise the Croat population itself, signally that it was acceptable to target them. This video also tells us that Hadzic knew about the negotiations between Croats and the JNA that were taking place down in Ilok, saying that he would be directly involved in talks about that. Hadzic knew about complaints about the intense war activities as they're described of local Serbs, Territorial Defence, and the JNA, but Hadzic brushed off complaints as "relatively justified." Hadzic believed that "we have to have a co-ordinated action between the people and the army." Your Honours, earlier I said the evidence would show that Goran Hadzic was a co-ordinator. He tells us that himself in this clip. His contribution was to ensure close co-ordination between, as he said, the people and the army. So far in these submissions, Your Honours, I have referred to several of the extermination and murder incidents that are charged in paragraphs 23 to 38 of the indictment, Counts 2 through 4. Time does not permit me to go into great detail on each of the remaining incidents. However, I would like to briefly mention them now. Considered altogether these show the pattern and the widespread and systematic nature of the attack on non-Serbs that was happening all across the region. I've spoken already about the 21st of September, 1991, incident when Goran Hadzic and Arkan came to the Dalj police station. Eleven non-Serb detainees were taken away and killed. Most of the bodies were later exhumed from Celije. The incident is charged in paragraph 24 of the indictment. About two weeks later, on the night of the 4th of October, Arkan and his men along with members of the local SBWS TO returned to the police station, interrogated and murdered approximately 28 non-Serb detainees from Baranja who had been brought to the detention facility by the Serb Special Police a few days earlier. Arkan and the other perpetrators then dumped the victims' bodies into the Danube River. When local residents of Dalj complained that their children could see the corpses floating down the river, Arkan publicly admitted to participating in the killing and promised that next time he would bury the bodies of the victims instead. That incident is charged in indictment paragraph 25. October 18th is the day of the Lovas minefield incident which I described earlier in my submissions. That is charged in paragraph 26. And then on the 9th of November, 1991, we've described the arrest and killing of the Pap, Kalozi, and Senasi men, and also then the killings that followed of Juliana Pap, her son, and Natalija Rakin after Juliana Pap went looking for her missing family members. Those incidents are charged in paragraphs 27 and 28 of the indictment. On the 11th of November, 1991, Arkan's Men came to the village of Klisa, east of Dalj, and arrested non-Serb employees of the DP Dalj company which was an agricultural enterprise for the region. Those non-Serbs had gathered there at the farm to receive their pay cheques. After enduring a night of brutal interrogations, Arkan's Men brought the detainees to the training centre at the government compound in Erdut. Two were released but the other five were executed. One other employee of the DP Dalj complained to Goran Hadzic about these arrests and the accused responded that it was none of his business and he refused to discuss the matter further. That's indictment paragraph 29. Your Honours, you've heard me refer several times now to the Erdut training centre and its proximity to the Hadzic government offices. This was without doubt the command centre for the crimes committed against the local non-Serb population. On the 10th of December, 1991, in addition to -- in addition to the incidents I've already described, on the 10th of December, the local police and TO, along with Arkan's Men, arrested five non-Serbs from Erdut and took them to the training centre and subsequently executed them. That's indictment paragraph 34. The scenario was repeated with grim familiarity on the 26th of December with regard to seven ethnic Hungarians and Croats. That's on page 35. Excuse me, indictment paragraph 35. And then again on the 21st of February, 1992, four members of the Albert family, Djuro, Helena, Viktorija, and mother-in-law Ana Terzic, age 76, they were killed after being taken to the training centre. That's charged in indictment paragraph 36. On the 4th of May, 1992, in the small village of Grabovac in the Baranja region of the SBWS, members of the Red Berets arrested five Croat and Hungarian civilians, including two women, Ruza Grofec and Andja Vlahovic and killed them. Their bodies were found in the Tikves Park in Beli Manastir near where the Red Berets were based. This is charged in indictment paragraph 37. Finally, Your Honours, you'll recall that at the beginning of my presentation I described the 9 November 1991 incident in which a number of the men from the Pap, Kalozi and Senasi families why killed. On the 3rd of June, 1992, Marija Senasi, the wife, mother, or mother-in-law of three of those men who had been killed earlier in 1991, she was executed by members of Goran Hadzic's security unit, the SNB, who were working with Arkan's Men. Her offence was the same as Juliana Pap's. She'd asked too many questions about the fate of her missing family members. Altogether, the incident of murder and extermination as charged in the indictment span September 1991 to June of 1992. The indictment lists 348 victims of murder and extermination during that period, but there are still some murder and extermination incidents charged in the indictment that I've not yet mentioned, and those are linked to Vukovar. During 1991, Croatian armed forces such as the Croatian National Guard had blockaded JNA barracks in different parts of Croatia, including the JNA barracks in Vukovar. After an earlier attempt to lift the blockade had failed, the JNA succeeded in deblocking its Vukovar barracks in early October 1991. After the Vukovar JNA barracks was de-blocked, the JNA demanded that the Croatian fighters in Vukovar lay down their arms. The Croats refused to surrender. This then gave rise to one of the most brutal and destructive battles that occurred in the wars of the former Yugoslavia, the battle for Vukovar. After the Croats refused to surrender, the JNA laid siege to the town, cutting off water and power while pounding the city with artillery and even aerial bombing. The population of Vukovar went underground, holing up in basement during what would be a seven-week siege. As Hadzic himself indicated in the video-clip played earlier, the battle for Vukovar was fought street by street, house by house. When it was over, the town and its structures were completely destroyed. Before it all started, the municipality of Vukovar was populated by 84.000 people, 43 per cent Croats, 38 per cent Serbs, with the remainder declaring themselves to be Hungarians, Muslims, and other groups or nationalities. Despite the fact that Croats were the largest ethnic group, Vukovar was nonetheless slated to be the capital of the SAO SBWS. Vukovar was to be taken so it could be a Serb town. The 18th of November, 1991, marks the fall of the city of Vukovar with the surrender of the last pockets of Croatian resistance. The siege and battle for Vukovar, its fall to Serb forces on the 18th and the terror and the violence that reigned in the days that follow have all been closely examined in previous cases in this Tribunal going all the way back to the trial of Slavko Dokmanovic that ended in June of 1998. When Vukovar fell, he was the minister of agriculture in Hadzic's SBWS government. Dokmanovic committed suicide here shortly before his judgement was announced. Your Honours, I'd like to run a short video-clip now that gives the Chamber an idea, an impression of what the town of Vukovar looked like after the battle was over. This footage is from late 1991 after Vukovar fell, so this would be within a month or so after the fall of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In the final days before Vukovar fell, hundreds of civilians and Croatian combatants who had laid down their arms sought refuge at the Vukovar Hospital, as rumours circulated that an evacuation supervised by the international community would take place from the hospital. The JNA took control of the hospital on the 19th, despite an agreement reached between the JNA and the Croatian government which placed the hospital under the protection of the ICRC and the -- during the -- for the duration of the evacuation. The JNA and the Croatian government also agreed that the ECMM would monitor the entire operation, the ECMM being the European Community Monitoring Mission. This is a photograph of the Vukovar Hospital from this period. The evacuation or removal of the Croat population from Vukovar was to take place on November 20. That morning, the JNA ordered men and women out of the hospital. Men were separated from women and children. The scene in Vukovar was chaos as the Serb forces, including volunteers and Chetniks, some of them drunk, moved through the town rounding up the non-Serb population as they emerged from their cellars. These are photos of the women and children from the day. After the Croat men were separated from the women and children, about 200 of them, men, were loaded onto five buses lined up outside the hospital. Representatives of the ICRC and the ECMM were trying -- were in Vukovar trying desperately to get to the hospital so they could monitor the treatment of the Croats being removed. However, they were prevented by the JNA from reaching the hospital before the five busloads of prisoners had left. The buses drove to the JNA barracks in Vukovar and remained parked there for several hours with the detained men on board. Serb TO members and paramilitaries milled around the buses and started to threaten and verbally abuse the men on the buses. A sixth bus arrived shortly thereafter. Beatings began. While the buses were being held at the JNA barracks, a meeting was held at another place called Velepromet outside of Vukovar between members of the SAO SBWS government and members of the JNA. We see the location of the hospital, the JNA barracks, and the Velepromet facility on this slide. This meeting at Velepromet was to decide the fate of the 200 men being held at the JNA barracks. Goran Hadzic, as president of the government of the SAO SBWS, attended the meeting. He came to the meeting with Arkan. Hadzic and other government members insisted that the Croat prisoners must remain in Vukovar, claiming that they would be prosecuted before local courts. Shortly after Vukovar fell, a first group of about 200 prisoners had already been transported down to the prison at Sremska Mitrovica in Serbia. The evidence will show that Goran Hadzic was firmly opposed to any more prisoners leaving the SBWS. Your Honour, this slide relates to the incident -- one of the additional murder and extermination incidents here charged in paragraph 31. The Velepromet facility where the meeting was held on the 20th of November was itself a detention facility where hundreds of Croats were being detained and beaten on the 19th, 20th, and 21st of November, 1991. Paragraph 31 of the indictment refers to the 17 prisoners who were killed there. Some prisoners refer to the room of death at Velepromet, a room where prisoners were kept before they were killed. Many of the prisoners at Velepromet were later transferred to the Sremska Mitrovica prison in Serbia, and I will speak about that shortly. Your Honours, this clip is also from the 20th of November, 1991. Here we see Hadzic, Arkan and other members of Hadzic's government and the JNA at the Velepromet facility. The parties have agreed that Arkan had accompanied Hadzic to the Velepromet meeting. In this footage, we see Hadzic giving an interview, and in close proximity we see Arkan along with others. I should say that we don't need translation or interpretation for this. It's just the images we'd like to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm going to pause briefly here, Your Honours. Your Honours will see this is Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, and Your Honours will also be able to identify Mr. Hadzic in the background. The next video-clip is from an interview that Goran Hadzic gave later, shortly after the Velepromet meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Goran Hadzic: This is the first session of the government held in the future capital of our Serb region of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem. As for the conclusions, apart from the ones relating to normalisation of life and creation of a more or less normal situation, the main conclusion is that the prisoners, the Ustashas with blood on their hands must not leave the territory of the Serbian district of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem and cannot go to Serbia, cannot be taken there because Serbia is not a country at war. Also, the troops that helped capture them, they ... the captured persons are not soldiers. They are members of paramilitary formations. They can only be put on trial by the people here, that is to say the people of our Serbian district which has been recognised, has its court, even a court of second instance. The third instance might possibly be at the federal level, at Yugoslav level. And we have our District Court and our Municipal Court. Consequently, we have agreed with the military authorities that these Ustasha remain in some of our camps here in the vicinity of Vukovar. Since one group was already taken to Sremska Mitrovica, I undertook the task of bringing these people back, if we can call them people. We shall bring them back, put them on trial, those who are guilty. Those who are not guilty will of course be released so they can join us in the reconstruction of our town."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
