utterances.text: Your Honours, in this video-clip, Goran Hadzic himself tells us the central role that he played in keeping those prisoners in the SBWS and preventing their removal to Serbia. As he says, "we have agreed with the military authorities that those Ustasha remain in some of our camps here in the vicinity of Vukovar." Since one group was already taken to Sremska Mitrovica," he says, "I undertook the task to return those people, if they can be called people," and "to put them on trial." With these words, Hadzic tells us that he has taken responsibility for these prisoners. He and his civilian authorities have assumed custody of them from the military authorities. The fact that Hadzic questions whether they can be called people signals the quality of justice that they can expect to receive in the SBWS. Your Honours, the evidence will show that once Hadzic succeeded in persuading the JNA to turn those 200 men over to him and his people, despite his promises of trials and justice, their fate was never in doubt. We've already heard what Arkan's policy was in respect of prisoners. The buses with the 200 or so Vukovar prisoners left the JNA barracks between 1.00 and 2.00 in the afternoon on the 20th of November and were escorted by military police of the JNA Operative Group South headed to the farming village of Ovcara located 5 or 6 kilometres from Vukovar. The buses arrived at a large hangar facility used to store farm equipment. The detained men were ordered into the hangar. While making their way in from the buses, they had to pass through a gauntlet composed of TO soldiers and members of paramilitary formations who kicked and punched the Croat prisoners as they passed through. A local farmer was ordered to take his front-end loader and dig a pit in a field that was less than 2 kilometres away from the hangar. Severe beatings continued inside the hangar facility for the rest of the afternoon and into the evening of the 20th. At least two prisoners died there. In the evening, they started transporting the prisoners in groups of 10 and 20 in a small truck out to the site where the pit had been dug. The killings took place over several hours extending beyond midnight into the early morning hours of November 21st, 1991. The men were lined up at the pit and executed. Altogether, 260 were killed or executed. The remains of 194 victims were recovered from the mass grave in 1996. That incident is charged in paragraph 32 of the indictment. Other Vukovar prisoners were transported towards Dalj on the 19th, 20, and 21st of November. When they reached Borovo Selo, two buses were stopped by members of the local TO and redirected to an enterprise called Lovas farms which actually is located near Dalj, not Lovas. Several of the detainees were killed at this Lovas farms facility. Other Vukovar prisoners were taken to Dalj and held in hangars belonging to the DPK Dalj company where they were mistreated and beaten. Some of them were killed. In total at least 35 of these detainees were executed and dumped into mass graves at Lovas farms and in Dalj. This is charged in paragraph 33 of the indictment. Your Honour -- Your Honours, I would now like to address the detention facilities and describe some of the detention crimes that are charged in Counts 5 through 9 of the indictment. These counts, Your Honours, charge Hadzic with crimes based on the mistreatment of non-Serbs who were arrested in the SBWS and detained in various detention facilities located not only in the SBWS but in Serbia also. The detention sites are listed in paragraph 41 of the indictment. The evidence will be that the prisoners were held and mistreated not only at detention facilities set up close to their own homes or places where they were arrested; for example, the training centre in Erdut or the Zadruga building in Lovas that I've already mentioned, but also these -- these facilities in Serbia. A number of these sites were the last known locations of the victims of murder and extermination that we've already mentioned. This first series of slides will indicate the locations of the detention facilities in the territory of the SBWS. There were police buildings and hangar in Dalj. The Erdut training centre that I've mentioned now repeatedly. And then some sites, detention sites located to -- or linked to the fall of Vukovar, the hospital, the JNA barracks, the Ovcara farm where the beatings occurred in the hangar before the prisoners were executed, and also the Velepromet facility where the meeting was held on the 20th of November, 1991, or -- and where prisoners were beaten and killed as well. There was the detention site in the town of Opatovac, and also in Borovo Selo, a workshop or a stable that was used. And finally, as I've mentioned, the Zadruga building in Lovas. Beatings and mistreatment occurred in all of these places. We now move to the detention facilities that were located in Serbia. These are the Stajicevo farm, the agricultural complex in Begejci, the military barracks in Zrenjanin, the military prison at Sremska Mitrovica that Hadzic refers to in the video-clip we just saw. He went to this prison. And also the military prison at Sid, across the river in Serbia. Some of these prisons had hundreds of detainees, others had smaller numbers. The non-Serb detainees in all of these facilities arrived in different ways. As we've heard, several of these places are associated with the fall of Vukovar. One other place that the Chamber will hear evidence about is the Borovo commerce shelter where around 1.500 Vukovar residents, including women and children, were taken prisoner. After the shelter was set on fire, many of these detainees, including the women and children, were transferred to the Borovo primary school where they were interrogated and mistreated before being expelled from the SBWS. The Chamber will hear evidence that Goran Hadzic dressed in a military uniform came to the Borovo primary school looking for a particular prisoner. Others were arrested and held in these places for interrogations, often before being killed. Many of the prisoners were people arrested and imprisoned by the Serb forces as they took control of their towns and villages across the SBWS during the late summer and autumn of 1991. People who couldn't flee or who simply had no where else to go were eventually rounded up and shipped off to these places. The prisoners were not just men of military age. Civilians, elderly, and women were victims of murder as we've seen. They were also victims of this unlawful imprisonment and mistreatment. Many of them were moved around between multiple centres over the course of days, weeks, and months. From day to day they didn't know where they -- excuse me. They did not know when and where they would be taken or what would await them when they arrived. Simply being moved from one detention centre to another posed a risk of death or injury. Prisoners were beaten during transfers by guards and were even tormented by locals on the road who had been told on the radio that the Ustashas would be passing through. They rocked the buses at threw stones at the terrified prisoners. To be transferred to a new detention facility meant being subjected to new beatings and other forms of mistreatment. In these prisons the detainees suffered every form of mistreatment and abuse. Prisoners were tortured by JNA officers and military police. Women suffered sexual violence. Prisoners were forced to beat other prisoners. Some were tormented by mock executions or forced to dig large holes which, they were told, would be their own graves. When prisoners died from their injuries, nothing was done. Apart from the beatings and mistreatment, the conditions in these places were horrible. There was overcrowding and outbreaks of lice. Prisoners were only permitted to shower right before the arrival of TV crews or the ICRC. They suffered from malnutrition and inadequate medical care. Doctors who were held prisoner themselves made requests for medical supplies but these were ignored as the conditions of the prisoners deteriorated further. Goran Hadzic went to Sremska Mitrovica prison, and he would have seen the conditions there. The survivors of these detention crimes, those who lived to be exchanged or released, still suffer permanent impairment due to the physical and psychological trauma they endured. Many were held for months only to be released in such poor condition that they spent years trying to recover from their injuries. Your Honours will hear the evidence of men and women who still live with debilitating conditions and serious disabilities resulting from their imprisonment in these facilities. Your Honour, I would now like to briefly address Counts 12 to 14, which charge Goran Hadzic with individual criminal responsibility for the crimes of destruction and plunder, including the destruction of religious sites. As the Serb forces took control of the villages and towns across the SBWS, killing or driving out the non-Serb inhabitants, what they didn't destroy, they took for themselves. In this, the JNA and its commanders co-ordinated closely with other units, including Arkan's Men. They were also reinforced by two other groups notorious for looting property from non-Serb homes. These were the JNA reservists and the Serbian volunteers dispatched by Seselj's Serbian Radical Party. After their owners were killed, the Erdut homes of the Kalozi and the Albert families, the Trial Chamber has already heard those names, as well as the homes of others killed by Serb forces, these homes were all taken over by Serbs. The Chamber will hear that after Arkan's Men killed one woman -- excuse me, Arkan's Men killed one man, a lorry arrived at the man's house to remove his possessions. In Erdut, a group that called itself the Refugees Protection Committee of the TO staff gave Serb refugees the homes of Croats and non-Serbs. This committee exercised its authority over the remaining non-Serbs by issuing orders to vacate property immediately. Some victims' homes were occupied by Arkan's Men. In the towns of Western Srem such as Sarengrad, Lovas, Tovarnik and Bapska, the JNA drove the local populations out with heavy artillery, tank and mortar fire. After the towns were destroyed and the people fled, many of them to Ilok, the Serb forces systematically plundered their homes. The evidence will show that Serb forces and Arkan in particular targeted, damaged, and destroyed religious and cultural structures such as Catholic churches and mosques in various locations during this period as well as in 1992 and 1993. Your Honours, at this point I would like to move on to 1992, where significant developments occurred with the acceptance and implementation of the Vance Plan, also the establishment of the RSK and Goran Hadzic's election as its president. As the violence and crime escalated inside the SBWS during the months I've just described, August through November 1991, the international community became increasingly involved in efforts to stop the violence, broker a cease-fire and protect civilian populations that were being terrorised and uprooted from their towns and villages throughout Croatia. Your Honours have already seen this map. The conflicts between Croats and Serbs weren't just taking place in the SAO SBWS in late 1991 but also in the SAOs of Krajina and Western Slavonia. Croats and non-Serbs were not the only victims. Large numbers of ethnic Serbs were driven out of their homes and villages in areas under Croat control. This was especially true in the SAO Western Slavonia where the areas under Serb control fell far short of the borders declared for the SAO Western Slavonia. By late 1991, war and ethnic cleansing had driven thousands, Croats and Serbs alike, from their homes. In Geneva, on the 23rd of November, 1991, five days after the fall of Vukovar, UN special envoy Cyrus Vance obtained signatures of Serbian President Milosevic, Croatian President Tudjman, and General Kadijevic on a cease-fire agreement that eventually served as the basis for what became known as the Vance Plan. I'd like to provide a brief overview of the Vance Plan, because it is tied to several important developments that impact this case throughout 1992 and 1993. Apart from the cease-fire, these were the main aspects of the plan. UN protected areas, or UNPAs, were to be established in Croatia. The territory of the four UNPAs would correspond generally to the territory of the three SAOs. As Your Honours can see, UNPA Sector East on this map corresponds quite closely to what we now know is the territory of the SAO SBWS. Under the Vance Plan, UNPA Sector North and Sector South corresponded roughly, quite closely but not precisely, to the territory of what had been the SAO Krajina. And then, thirdly, UNPA Sector West corresponded to the territory of the SAO Western Slavonia, again although it extended beyond territory controlled by the Serbs there. Under the Vance Plan, these UNPAs were to be demilitarised, and people living within those UNPAs were to be protected by a United Nations Protection Force called UNPROFOR, consisting of military personnel and civilian police. The protection force became known colloquially as the Blue Helmets. The JNA and other military personnel from Serbia were to withdraw under the Vance Plan, and the local police would be responsible for maintaining law and order. Importantly, displaced persons, that is people who'd been expelled from their homes or who'd fled, would be allowed to return. In late 1991, among the Serb leadership, Slobodan Milosevic supported the plan. After initially opposing it, Goran Hadzic joined Milosevic in supporting the plan for the SBWS, although, as we will see, he did not accept the provision for allowing non-Serbs to return or on demilitarisation. Milan Babic, the leader of the SAO Krajina, remained strongly opposed to the plan. The evidence will show that his refusal to support the Vance Plan cost Babic the support of Milosevic and Belgrade. The evidence will show that this led to Hadzic's elevation to the position of president of the RSK in late February 1992, and I'll speak about that in a few minutes. Another reason why the Vance Plan is significant for this case is because by the spring of 1992, the first UNPROFOR personnel began arriving in the UNPAs; that is, within the territory of the SAOs in Croatia. This meant that for the first time since the conflict began, internationals would be present in the very areas where the crimes that I've been discussing this morning were taking place. In carrying out their mandate, the UNPROFOR personnel began seeing things, hearing things, meeting with local authorities, and most importantly writing reports. During the trial, the Chamber will hear the evidence of international staff who -- and will have the benefit of the reports written by them and their colleagues. The Chamber will have evidence that the persecution and expulsion of non-Serbs from the Serb-held territories in Croatia continued throughout 1992 and 1993. There's one last series of important political developments that I'd like to mention. In late 1991, Babic and the leadership of the SAO Krajina formally declared that SAO to be a republic called the republic of -- excuse me, Republic of Srpska Krajina, RSK. On the 26th of February, 1992, as preparations were underway for the UN Protection Force to begin deploying into the UNPAs under the Vance Plan, Croatian Serb leaders of the SAO SBWS and Western Slavonia met at Borovo Selo where they decided to join the RSK. At this time, amendments to the RSK constitution were adopted, a government was formed, and Goran Hadzic was elected president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. As president now of the republic, by the 26th of February, 1992, these were some of Hadzic's powers and responsibilities under the RSK constitution: He could proclaim laws by edict; he performed duties in the domain of foreign affairs between RSK and other states and international institutions; and he commanded the armed forces in peace and during a state of war, and also commanded the national resistance during a state of war; he could issues orders for general and partial mobilisation. And so beginning in February of 1992, there was a significant change in the nature of the conflict between Croats and Serbs, the size of the territory over which Hadzic has authority, and the nature of his powers. The nature of the conflict changed because with the establishment of the UNPAs and the arrival of the Blue Helmets, the confrontation lines remained fairly stable, although there was continued armed conflict between Serb and Croatian forces throughout the remaining time-frame for our case, 1992 and 1993. The size of the territory over which Hadzic had authority increased substantially, because as president of the RSK, his authority now extended throughout the combined territories of what had been SAO Krajina, SAO Western Slavonia, and SAO SBWS. Hadzic enjoyed an expansion of his de jure powers under the RSK constitution. One thing, however, did not change. The evidence will show that Hadzic's policy on populations within the RSK was no different than his policy in the SAO SBWS. He rejected co-existence with Croats and non-Serbs in the areas under Serb control. He embraced the Vance Plan only as a way to preserve the status quo of Serb-held territory in Croatia. Throughout 1992 and 1993, non-Serbs continued to be persecuted and expelled from the RSK. Despite his public support for the Vance Plan, Hadzic did not support the return of non-Serb refugees into areas under Serb control. RSK policy was to prevent their return. I'd like to briefly address Hadzic's role as president of the RSK during this period. As we've seen, under the RSK constitution, Hadzic was essentially Commander-in-Chief of the armed forces, but under the Vance Plan, the RSK wasn't supposed to have military forces, just police forces. With the proclamation of the RSK, Territorial Defence forces were formed and under the RSK constitution, they were subordinated to Hadzic. In contravention of the Vance Plan, the Serbian military and police organs that were supposed to withdraw under the Vance Plan instead turned over their military equipment to the newly formed RSK TO units, and even some JNA personnel remained and served in the RSK Territorial Defence. These RSK police continued to be financed, trained, and equipped by Serbia, including the Serbian Ministry of Interior. When UNPROFOR was deployed to Croatia in May of 1992, many of the RSK TO units were then transformed into these Special Police units, since under the Vance Plan the police were the only authorities authorised to be present in the UNPAs. Instead of withdrawing or demobilising, JNA and RSK Territorial Defence commanding officers, personnel, and equipment were transformed to these newly formed Special Police Units. Even JNA and TO vehicles were repainted to make them into police vehicles. Also in violation of the Vance Plan, on the 18th of May, 1992, Hadzic as president promulgated a decision establishing the Serbian Army of the RSK called the SVK. Not surprisingly, the SVK relied heavily on financial, logistical and operational support from the Yugoslav army and Serbia's political leadership. Also contrary to the Vance Plan undertaken on demilitarisation, Arkan's Tigers arrived in Knin from the SBWS and fought there in early 1993. They were an integral part of the SVK. Goran Hadzic's role during this period as Commander-in-Chief of the SVK is illustrated here in the military rally held in July of 1992. The occasion is Hadzic's promotion of Milan Martic and Colonel Borislav Djukic to the rank of General of the SVK.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Goran Hadzic: May God be with you. "The public: May God be with you. "Goran Hadzic: I greet you all in the name of all citizens of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and please allow me to thank you for all you have done for us all. You, standing here before us, you are the new Obilics and Sindjelics, the new heros whose actions will be written about in the history books of the Serbian people. Your brothers and ours who gave their lives will go down in history as saints, and their blood spilled for the freedom of the Serbian people is holy. Through this act which you have carried out, we have shown that the Serbian people have never been on their knees and have never asked anybody for mercy, that we can accomplish all we want by ourselves. And from this place here, we send a joint message to all the wheelers and dealers of the world that the Republic of Serbian Krajina is not for sale. No price can be put on our freedom, and we will not sell it for any money in the world. We are now in a very difficult situation, encircled on all sides by our enemies, but we have never yet been so unified and decisive to defend our freedom. Most importantly, we are aware of our enemies and nobody can fool the Serbian people anymore with some new 'brotherhood and unity,' some new deceits. All citizens of the Republic of Serbian Krajina are equal and will be equal regardless of their ethnicity but it must be known that this is the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and those who accept that can live here. Those who do not want to can leave the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Now, I don't want to tire our brave troops in this sun anymore. I would like to thank them once again and to publicly announce here for the first time that as of today we have two new generals of the Serbian Army. They are Borislav Djukic and Milan Martic. Long live and thank you."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the evidence will show that during 1992 and 1993; Martic and Djukic were among the RSK authorities, both civilian and military, led by the accused, who implemented persecutory policies to remove the remaining non-Serbs from the Serb-held territories, while at the same time preventing those already expelled from returning. While thousands of non-Serb residents had been killed or fled during 1991, those who remained were targeted. The non-Serbs living in the RSK suffered abuses ranging from losing their jobs and freedom of movement to losing their homes and even their lives. One UN official said that they were subjected to a "prolonged and consistent pattern of intimidation." Discrimination against the non-Serbs of the RSK was part of the wider programme of ethnic cleansing, one purpose of which was to free up houses for Serbs being welcomed from other areas. Those who remained were extremely vulnerable and were preyed upon by the Serb forces as they were repeatedly robbed and their property taken. You will hear testimony that the RSK leadership ensured that even when non-Serb farmers were owed money for their crops, the local co-operative was ordered not to give them the food coupons they'd earned. The effect was they could not feed their families. You will hear evidence from an UNPROFOR official in Beli Manastir located in the Baranja portion of SBWS, that non-Serbs slept outside the headquarters of the Belgian UNPROFOR peacekeepers there because they were afraid of the violence they would face by Serb forces if they returned to their homes. The ranking UNPROFOR official in Sector East, the SBWS region, will describe the expulsions of non-Serbs he witnessed from the towns of Erdut and Aljmas on the 11th of April, 1992. Elderly people, women and children, were forcibly removed from their homes and forced to leave their possessions behind, loaded onto buses bound for Croat-held territory at gunpoint. When confronted about these crimes, the RSK authorities made half-hearted attempts to characterise the departure as voluntary. Another UNPROFOR official raised the issue of expulsions directly with Hadzic in April 1992. Hadzic's response was to demand that the accusers be brought directly to him or to refer to centuries of oppression suffered by Serbs as though that was a form of justification for what was taking place. The Chamber will hear evidence of several UN officials about the destruction and plunder of non-Serb property that continued during 1992 and 1993. Churches and mosques were also targeted. The JNA and Serb forces targeted and caused extensive damage to the churches in Sarengrad, Erdut, Dalj, Tovarnik, Bapska, and Aljmas. The destruction of places of warship continued even after UNPROFOR's deployment. In the fall of 1992, UNPROFOR received reports on the destruction of churches near Knin and other parts of that area. In 1993, another UNPROFOR official noticed an increase in attacks on churches in Sector East culminating in April of that year. This official complained bitterly to the RSK authorities in April 1993 when rockets were fired at the church in Ilok and a bomb was detonated on the steps of the Ilok monastery. The destruction of these religious buildings served no military purpose. Rather, Serb forces intentionally destroyed them in order to show the non-Serbs that as a people, a community, they no longer had a place in this Republic of Serbian Krajina. Their places of worship, symbolic of one of their defining characteristics as a group, ceased to exist. And so what was the end result of all of this crime, murder and expulsion that occurred in the areas of the SBWS and the RSK under Goran Hadzic? The demographic evidence to be presented at the trial will show that the territories of the SBWS and Krajina were overall ethnically mixed in March of 1991, with a similar proportion of Serbs and Croats overall, with some ethnic minorities as well. Your Honours have heard about Hungarians and also Slovaks. However, some of the areas such as Wester Srem and Baranja had a relatively small number of Serbs. The area of Vukovar was roughly 43 per cent Croat and 38 per cent Serb before the conflict. To transform these regions into essentially ethnic Serb territories would require huge numbers of people to be moved out, expelled. The evidence is going to show that that is exactly what happened during Goran Hadzic's tenure, first as prime minister of the SBWS and then as president of the RSK. The evidence will show that hundreds of thousands, at least 180.000 people were forcibly expelled from these territories between the 25th of June, 1991, when Hadzic was designated to be the leader of the SBWS government and 31 December 1993, which is the end of Hadzic's tenure as president of the RSK. Over 90 per cent, 97 per cent of these people were ethnic Croats and non-Serbs. In Vukovar alone, roughly 20.000 people were expelled after the city fell to Serb forces; 97.9 per cent of them were non-Serbs. Vukovar was to be the capital of the SBWS. On the 2nd of March, 1992, shortly after he became president of the RSK, Goran Hadzic attended a meeting of the SFRY Presidency held in Belgrade. He was accompanied by a man named Zdravko Zecevic, who was the RSK prime minister, the leader of the RSK government. Also present at this meeting were Milan Martic and Mr. Paspalj, who had travelled with Mr. Hadzic to New York in early 1993 in the video footage that we saw earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, it's about that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I can finish in about five minutes, Your Honour. If we could -- if I could -- I can come back and conclude, but I've literally got about one page left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise. I thought we were going to go another hour and a half. I forgot about the 15. The meeting on -- on March 2nd, 1992, at the Presidency in Belgrade was attended, as I've said, by Hadzic, Martic, Paspalj, and the RSK Prime Minister Zecevic. This is what Zecevic said about the idea that Croats driven from the town of Benkovac might actually return as was envisioned under the Vance Plan. And I apologise for the long quote, Your Honours, but I would like to read it. Mr. Zecevic said: "It is not my intention to bother you with specific situation in Benkovac, but this town is specific when it comes to refugees. We are thinking only about our refugees, and we would like them to come back, and they are welcome here. I'm in panic when I think that 15.000 Croats would return to Benkovac, and they are mostly peasants emotionally linked to the soil. They are now compacted in Zadar area, along the coastal area. I fear the excess ignited by our people. This issue is a complex one. The instinct made our people burn anything that belonged to Croats in order to prevent them from coming back to their homes. The truth is that we cannot live together, that we do not want to live with them any more. But there is also another type of truth which is recognised by a democratic world and which claims that these people have the right to return to their homes. I really cannot imagine how we're going to organise life then; I guess we'll have to think about it later. I'm picturing it like this - well, gentlemen, the schools will teach Cyrillic, and you will hate it so much that you will simply have to leave. That is what is awaiting us." Your Honours, the evidence will show that Mr. Zecevic's candid words about the prospects for those peasants emotionally tied to the soil actually being allowed to come to their homes and work their land, statements made while his president, Goran Hadzic, sat silently nearby, are in fact an accurate statement of the RSK government policy under Hadzic. In Hadzic's RSK, only Serbs were welcome. At the end of 1993, Goran Hadzic lost a general election to Milan Martic, who then took over to become the president of the RSK. In 1995, the RSK and the territories in Croatia claimed as Serb autonomous territory all disappeared. Croatia re-took the areas of the SAO Western Slavonia and Krajina in operations called Flash and Storm. The territory of what has been the SAO SBWS was gradually reintegrated into Croatia after the signing of the Erdut agreement in late 1995. Even in Goran Hadzic had not succeeded in creating a permanent Serbian entity or state in Croatia, the evidence will show that he did at least during the time that he was in power succeed with his JCE members in separating Serbs from non-Serbs there. This was achieved by the commission of many crimes, the crimes charged in the indictment in this case. We thank Your Honours for your attention. At the end of this trial, the Prosecution will return to ask that the Chamber find Goran Hadzic guilty of the crimes he is charged with in this case as set out in Counts 1 through 14 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stringer. We will now break and come back at 12.50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I understood that -- we understood that there will be no declaration from the Defence pursuant to Rule 84 nor a statement from Mr. Hadzic pursuant to 84 bis. So the Prosecution can call their first witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I could introduce to the Chamber Ms. Lisa Biersay. She's an extremely experienced advocate for the Prosecution in this Tribunal. She's appeared in other trials. She'll be appearing regularly in this trial, and I think the Chamber knows -- and some you know our Case Manager, Thomas Laugel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. My sincere apologies. I failed to mention Muireann Dennehy, who is also a legal officer in the Office of the Prosecution, and I should have introduced her to Your Honours as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. I am hoping to address the issue of some exhibits that we propose to show to this witness. They are new exhibits, and they were addressed with him during his proofing on the 14th and 15th of October. This is my first appearance before the Trial Chamber, and I am also bringing a motion that I understand is perhaps not going to be granted in full. And with that knowledge, I would like to address those exhibits, if I may, with the Trial Chamber before the witness comes into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you do that -- sorry. Could you do that in more or less five minutes, Ms. Biersay?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honours. It will be brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So we are seeking leave to add to our Rule 65 ter exhibit list certain exhibits, and as I said, these were discussed with -- with the witness over the weekend. Essentially at issue we have three maps, one drawn by the witness, one is a basic road map, and a close-up of a segment of that road map. We had other maps available for him to use, but he was much more comfortable with the traditional map which is not on our 65 ter exhibit list. I did manage to speak to Defence counsel, and they're not objecting to the map that was hand drawn by him, and that would be 65 ter -- the proposed 65 ter exhibit number is 6328, which I believe is your tab 1. So I don't believe there are any objections to the addition of that one. Then we also have some photographs that the witness identified as places where he was in Dalj and in Erdut. Three of the photographs are essentially of the same place, just different angles. And one photograph is a Google photograph of a place where he was in Erdut, and so the ones pertaining to Dalj would be your tabs. I believe, if I'm correct, it would be your tabs 4, 5, and 6; so our 65 ter number 6331, 6332, and 6333. And then the Google Earth map would be proposed 65 ter number 6253. So we found that it was helpful to the -- to the witness to describe where he was, what level, what room. It was helpful for his explanation of what he experienced. And so we would propose that they be added to the 65 ter list and we be allowed to use those exhibits with him. There is another exhibit that was subject to the third motion to amend our 65 ter exhibit list. The Defence indicated that they would object to this exhibit because it was very long and they hadn't had sufficient time to look at it. So I am proposing at that we defer addressing the issue of that exhibit today, and I will endeavour to meet with the Defence after today's session and show them that we're merely seeking to add less than a five-minute segment of that 40-minute video, and we're seeking to do it without any sound. So essentially it's for the moving images for which we would seek to add and tender the -- that -- that exhibit. And from that exhibit the witness identified some people that he recognised. So for purposes of -- of today, we have 65 ter number 6328, which is the one agreed upon by the Defence. Then we have 6329, 6330, 6331, 6332, and 6333. There's another one, but we're happy to just be focused on the very core ones for purposes of addition to the 65 ter exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If I'm not wrong, Ms. -- could you please recall me the pronunciation of your name.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Absolutely. I like to tell people that it sounds like Dutch beer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So it's Biersay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. So if I'm not wrong, you mentioned 65 ter number 6253 --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I wonder if I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But not in your last summary and I had a problem with that one.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Oh, excuse me, Your Honour. You're absolutely -- you're absolutely correct. And that would be your -- your tab 12. So you're correct. It would be your tabs 1 through 6 and then tab 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: 1 through 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Not 7 and 12 --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- right?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Correct. It's our effort to reduce it as much as we can without compromising what would assist in his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And then just to be totally clear, 6253, that number 12 --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- is in your list --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- is not mentioned as or not highlighted as new.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: No, it was not, but it is not new to the proposed exhibits for purposes of the Trial Chamber, but it's new because it's not yet on the 65 ter exhibit list. It's subject to our third motion to amend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Can we hear from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. First, I can confirm that after consulting with my learned friend that we did agree that there would be no objection to 6328. The second matter is the maps. Now, I suppose I should just pause here and try to convey what the principle is that the Defence would like to follow. If there is an existing document on the 65 ter list that is modified by the witness, we would have no objection to that. So what we would object to, however, Your Honour, are new maps or new materials being brought forward with the witness, and that would include not only the traditional maps that were apparently shown to the witness but also any, I guess, Google photos. And the Google photos we would object to not only on the basis that they're not on the 65 ter list but also that although Google can be very useful for certain issues and illustrating certain things, we don't think it's appropriate for photographs. We would object to tabs 4, 5, and 6 on the basis that although these are investigators' photographs, nonetheless they're new. We've got no notice of them. And, finally, we have the video, and we've expressed our position on that in an e-mail to the Chamber. I think that covers everything, but I'm at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think the video is not an issue yet, unless I'm wrong, because the Prosecution is still trying or will try to get an agreement from you on that -- on that one, and we will see that one tomorrow. We see about that one tomorrow, okay? So what you are saying is no problem for tab 1, 65 ter 6328. 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 you say, We object, and 12 you object as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We, of course, do not object to the 65 ter 6328, the parties agreeing upon that one. So we will allow the addition of that one, that exhibit to the 65 ter list. But for the other ones we are of the view that the Defence objections are justified and we will deny the motion.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. So at this time I think we're prepared to call the witness, Mr. Antunovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Can we call the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. What is your name and your date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zlatko Antunovic, 23rd of December, 1973.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please make the solemn declaration. The usher will assist you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please take a seat. Before -- before I give the floor to the Prosecution for your direct examination, could you please tell us what your ethnicity is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Antunovic.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I wanted to know if you were comfortable seated where you are. How does it feel, the chair?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Everything is fine, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you're able to hear me?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And if that changes, will you let us know, please?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Have you ever testified before?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Does that include local proceedings as well? Have you testified in local proceedings?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So this is your very first time.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: The first time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber asked you what your full name was, and you gave them that. Do you also have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: I do, "Kepa."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what does "Kepa" mean?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Like a person of a small stature, a midget, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When did you get that nickname?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Back in primary school.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How old were you then?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Nine.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber where you were born.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And did you grow up and go to school in Osijek or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: No. I grew up in Erdut, and I went to school at Dalj.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How -- do you remember how old you were when you moved to Erdut?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Sixteen, 17 when I moved to the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And Osijek and Erdut and Dalj, where are they, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay, can I -- can I have one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Antunovic, I forgot, and I have to tell you what the consequences are of your solemn declaration. You are obliged to tell the truth, nothing but the truth, and you expose yourself to perjury should you not do so. Thank you. Sorry, about that, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: No problems, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you tell us, generally speaking, where Osijek, Erdut, and Dalj are?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: In Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And is that in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Croatia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, when you moved to Erdut, did you live alone or did you live with someone else?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: I moved to the village of Erdut in 1989, and I lived there with my aunt and uncle.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where did you live with your parents?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: I lived outside of the village. There were three or four houses; a small hamlet we call Salas back in our parts, halfway between Erdut and Dalj.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So just so that I understand, you first lived with your parents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I lived with my parents. The address was Podvinje 21. That was the name of the street.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And this place where you lived with your parents, is that the place that was outside the -- the village, as you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the place.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And which village do you mean?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: This hamlet where you lived with your parents, approximately how many houses were there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: There were three households.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And do you know the ethnicity of those households?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: My neighbour was Croat, his wife was a Serb, and there was another neighbour of mine who was Ruthenian.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And could you describe for the Trial Chamber the relationship between neighbours in this hamlet where you lived with your parents.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Things were normal. We went along well. We helped each other out, and I mean my parents, of course. We had no problems whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you tell us the name of your parents, please.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: My father Josip and my mother Katica.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, you lived in this hamlet outside the village of Erdut. Did you go to school there or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: No. I went to school at Dalj.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how far was it from where you lived to school in Dalj?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Roughly 5 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how did you get to school?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: There was a school bus from Erdut to Dalj and onwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you some questions about your school, the one you went to in Dalj. Approximately how many students attended this -- this school?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you how many, but quite a few from Grade 1 to 8. There were four classes per every generation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And in your class specifically, could you describe the ethnic composition, make-up, of your class?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: The population was mixed. There were mostly Croat and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In Dalj itself, what was the ethnic composition of Dalj?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: It was mixed, but the majority was Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what about Erdut?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: There were many more Croats than Serbs in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Going back to your -- your school, how did you get along with your other classmates of other ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't have any problems. As children we never made such distinctions other than perhaps by who supported which football club. We didn't even know what politics meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you play football?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And was -- on the team, did you play with other children of other ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was mixed. They were all villages of Erdut, Dalj, whoever took part, Croats or Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, did you have a best friend while you were in school in Dalj?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I did. From my class they were Serbs and Croats. We were on good terms. We played as children. Everything was all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And your -- your -- did you have a best friend or did you have -- all your friends were the same?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: We socialised and played together without making such a distinction. There was no reason for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where you lived with your parents, did you play somewhere close by?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: We would often play at the holiday centre of the Osijek water supply company. There was a place where your could swim, and there was a playground. So we went and played there very often.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What was the name of this place?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: It's called Vodovod Osijek, or it was also called Pustara.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how close was that to your house where you lived with your parents?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: One kilometre or 1.5 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you describe what that -- you described it as a holiday centre. Could you describe what it looked like?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: There was one area where drinks were sold. There was a football pitch and a basketball court. Then there were huts that will we -- we called them like that, or bungalows, where people employed for the Osijek water supply company would come for holidays for 10 or 15 days. There was a park as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So close to the house where you lived with your parents there was the Vodovod which was nearby. Was there another company-related site that was close to your house there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was the IPK Osijek, the wine growing company where I worked.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you know the full name of the IPK?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Industrial and Agricultural Complex Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what did they do?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Grape growing. They had vineyards.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And do you know where they had their vineyards?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: I do. Next to Novi Erdut, roughly along the line of Bogaljevci which was a street in Erdut and then in the direction of the Erdut Planina area, or Mount Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time I'd like to call up 65 ter 6328, which is also tab 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Antunovic, there is water if you need to drink a little bit. It does get dry.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. It's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: While we wait for that exhibit -- can you see it on your screen?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document before you on that screen?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what do you recognise it to be?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: This is the area where Erdut, Bogaljevci and the water supply company centre -- is my home. The road to Aljmas and Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And do you recognise the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Does your name appear on that document?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Antunovic, if --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If Mr. Antunovic could be assisted with a pen just to point out the areas as he discusses them?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the top of that exhibit, 65 ter 6328, there is the word "Dunav." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what -- what is that? What is Dunav?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: It's the river that flows by Erdut, the Danube.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And could you use your pen to touch the area of Erdut.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And did you mark the part of the map that is the letter E?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what does that E represent? Is that all of Erdut or one part of Erdut?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: No. This is the centre of Erdut. All the rest comes under the village, but I marked the very centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, to the right of the E where you just placed the mark, what is that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: This is where the castle is. Beyond the castle there is the Erdut Winery, and then next to it there is an area that we called Predvojnicka. This is where Zeljko Raznjatovic's units were located.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, in the upper right-hand section there is the word -- is it "Srbija"?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is bridge across the Danube, and on the other bank of the river lies Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you point out for the Chamber, please, where the Vodovod was located?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you've marked the lower part of that map; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how are you able to -- let me start again. Are you able to put a pen at the approximate point where your parents' house was?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And could you read the words that appear next to that mark that you've just made on the lower right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: It reads "Parents' house."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now directing your attention to the middle of that map. "Vinogradi," what is that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: This is the area where the vineyard was planted stretching from Novi Erdut all the way to Osijek alongside Bogaljevci, all the way from the main road to Osijek through to the road to Dalj and Erdut Planina which ultimately reads to Aljmas.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you know anyone who has worked in those vineyards that you just highlighted for us?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And who do you know?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: There were many of them. Now, by name, for instance, Tihomir Majkic, Marinko Lucan, Pero -- well, apologies. I can't recall all the names.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: There were many of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you have any relatives who worked there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: There were relatives of mine. My cousin, Josip Antunovic, worked there, as did Ivan Albert, but he was the foreman or the boss, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In the area, can you estimate how -- what percentage of the people who lived in this area worked for the IPK vineyards?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, from our village of Erdut, between 60 and 70 per cent of all people worked there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And where did your father work?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: My father had worked for years before 1989 there. He worked for the IPK.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you know approximately for how long he worked there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Some 20 years for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did there come a time that you started working there as well?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Immediately upon completing my elementary education in September 1988, I went to pick grapes for the first time and then I continued working there on a seasonal basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How old were you when you first went to work for the vineyards?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Fifteen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You said you lived with your -- your parents at this address, and was there anybody else in the household?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My brother Goran was also a member of the household.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, looking at this map, how far would it be from your parents' house to the area that you've marked "Arkan"? Approximately how far would that be?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, around 5 kilometres. Between 4 and 5 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You can let the pen rest, Mr. Antunovic. If we need to, we'll come back to it. Thank you. What happened --

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You described your father and where you worked. Did your father have a view of what his ethnicity was? What did he consider himself as?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: He considered himself to be a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What does the word -- to describe someone as a Yugoslav, what does that mean to you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, a citizen of Yugoslavia. That person was Yugoslav in those terms, but by ethnicity he or she was Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did anyone in your family consider him or herself to be a Yugoslav?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, we were all Yugoslavs. We lived in that state, and my father respected Tito. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What happened to your parents in a caused you to move?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: They both died in 1989, my father in January and my mother in November. They suffered from cancer, both of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And where did you go to live next?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: I moved to stay with my mother's sister, my aunt, and her husband in the village of Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what were their names?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: My aunt's name is Anica or Ana Kristic, and my uncle's name is Stjepan Butkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And could you describe approximately where their house was in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Is it possible for us to clean the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If we move it now, Ms. Biersay, we will -- we will lose every marking.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Then I'd propose that we take a shot of it and save it and then call it up anew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can we do that, Mr. Registrar? Okay. It will be done.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And, Your Honour -- Your Honours, we would tender the -- both the marked version and the clean version into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's what I was waiting for, Ms. Biersay. Yes, please, to be marked. To be marked as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 6328 shall be marked as Exhibit P1, and 65 ter document 6328 marked by the witness in court shall be assigned Exhibit P2. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. So now if we could please have P1 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Antunovic, we're just trying to erase these markings so you can make new ones so you're not making markings on top of markings. There we go. So could you now point to Exhibit P1 and indicate approximately where your aunt and uncle lived. We'll help you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: It keeps moving. I can't.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: It's not a test, so don't worry.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So you've marked to the lower left of the E that is on your drawing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And approximately how far did they live from the Erdut centre as you described it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Some 300 metres. It was very close. It's a small village in total.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You described that there was harmonious relationships when you were going to school and in your village. What was the atmosphere like when you moved to live with your aunt and uncle as far as the interactions between the ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time things were still normal. If there was anything different, I still didn't feel it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And when did that change? When did that feeling of things being normal, when did that change for you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: I think in 1990, when the parties were established in the country, like the HDZ. I think it was then that many things changed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how did that show itself, that change? How did that show up in your daily life?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: I had many Serbian friends. Even my best friend was a Serb. On one occasion we had a conversation, and he told me that we would no longer socialise because I was a Croat, he was a Serb. I was with the HDZ youth, whereas he was a member of the SDS. And that we had nothing in common. It was along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you around this time get any special markings to show your membership with the HDZ youth?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had a HDZ tattoo on my right arm, a tattoo of the Croatian Democratic Union.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And when did you have that placed there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: In 1990, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And why did you get that tattoo?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I had friends who were members of the party, and I was a member of the party youth organisation. Basically there was no explanation. I just had it made. It turned out to have been a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: We'll -- we'll talk about that. Before I move to the next topic, I wanted to ask you if at some time -- at some point after 1990 you saw any military-related activities in your area of Erdut-Dalj.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1991, the National Guards Corps arrived in Erdut, Croatian soldiers, and there were some Croatian reserve policemen there as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And the -- I'm looking at the translation. You said the National Guards Corps arrived in Erdut, meaning the Croatian soldiers. And where did they go? Were they stationed somewhere in Erdut or around Erdut?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: They were stationed -- if we look at the map -- do you want me to indicate it?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: That would be --

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Where Arkan arrived later.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So perhaps you can put an X, if you've mastered the pen.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: If I can manage.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you have. Okay. So you're marking the "Arkan" box as being the place where the -- I want to say it exactly - the National Guard Corps was; right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were there and at the Vodovod facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you've also marked that with an X; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What did you see them doing, if anything?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I saw soldiers carrying rifles. They moved around the village much like the other civilians were. I guess they had some training of theirs, but I do distinctly remember seeing them about the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At some point in time did something happen to the Vodovod?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. During a night, the Vodovod area was shelled.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And do you remember the approximate month and year when that happened?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: It was in 1991, towards the end of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If you could take us back in time and describe how you experienced that event. What was the first thing that you remember happening that night in -- in late July 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: During the night, one could hear shells being fired and explosions. In any case, I remember my aunt pulling me down to the floor from my bed, and we stayed on the floor until things calmed down.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you -- could you tell at the time approximately from what direction these explosions were coming from?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, not at that moment. Later on I heard from some people that the shells were being fired from across the bridge, from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And is that bridge on your map, P1?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you mark it with an X, please.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And is it correct that you've managed it on the box marked "Most"?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And do you remember how long these explosions went on for?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember how long it all took. In any case, there were more than one explosion. There were more, but I don't know how long it all took.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What happened -- did you eventually go outside?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Once things calmed down, we went outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where did you go the next day -- or should I say that day? So it was night when the explosion started, and at the first light, that's what I -- that's what I mean by "next day."

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the morning, I accompanied the local firemen who were volunteers to the Vodovod facility to see what was there and to help. We wanted to help gather the property that was there. When we arrived there, we could see that it had been shelled. There was blood. We mainly gathered the mattresses where the Croatian soldiers used to sleep.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And where did you see blood?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: On the mattresses. They were on the floor in the wooden bungalows, and there was a stench.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And when you say "stench," what do you mean by "stench"?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: I guess the stench of burning and blood. I had never experienced such smell before. In any case, it was not in the least pleasant.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You describe the IPK being next to the Vodovod, that there was a facility in that area. Was there any damage to that as well?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, not at the vineyard. It had not been shelled.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were there any buildings near the Vodovod that had been shelled or damaged by the shelling, as far as you could tell?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, two, two buildings where the IPK had their tractors, agricultural equipment. A few shells landed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention to the time when you were told to -- to go home, where you couldn't go to work. You tried to go to work and you couldn't go to work. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the morning just like on any other working day, I went to the centre of Erdut, and from there --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I just wanted to know which -- what day are we talking about? Do you remember when that -- what you're about to describe? When you tried to go to work and you couldn't.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of August, 1991, I went to catch a bus which took us to the vineyards. Some people arrived, the police, and told us to go back home, that there was nothing to do and that the police station in Dalj had been attacked.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing. I turned back home.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you hear anything unusual on that day?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I heard that there were tanks arriving towards the village, and I realised that myself later on. There was much noise, and I could clearly tell that they weren't trucks or buses. On top of that, people were saying that JNA tanks had crossed over the bridge and were about to enter Erdut and move further afield.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And do you mean the same bridge that you've marked with the X over the word "Most"? Is that the bridge you mean?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you see the tanks yourself?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, not at that point in time when they entered.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What was the atmosphere like that day in the -- in the town?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Everyone was confused, and people went home. If they had cellars, they hid there. We had certain neighbours who came over to my uncle's house to hide in our cellar. Most of them, though, went in the direction of Aljmas, because they were told that there was a boat awaiting there to take them to safety, towards Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And approximately how many people sought refuge in your basement?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Sometimes there were four or five or six. It depended and changed. Some left while others stayed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what ethnicity were those people who sought refuge in your basement?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm looking at the clock, and I had hoped to -- to play a video, but I think it's best to keep it for tomorrow at this point, and I'll just finish up on this segment if that's okay with the Chamber. From here it looks like it's five to 2.00, and I'm just trying to think ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You could -- you could be right, Ms. Biersay. You'll lose five minutes. What's five minutes in life?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'll continue until I get the signal that it's time, and I'm happy to proceed that way, but I just wanted to let you know that I'm aware of the time, but I may not be able to find a stopping point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How -- you said you went home. How long did you stay in your house without going outside?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I stayed home. As I told you, some people went to Aljmas, whereas my uncle, aunt, and I stayed behind. The next six or seven days I was inside the house for the most part because I feared going outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you watch television during this time?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we watched television. There was some footage of Aljmas, and we could see people fleeing towards Osijek. There was also some reporting about events in the environs of Dalj.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you -- did you -- were you able to see any programmes from Serbian TV, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We could see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what were those reports about?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't remember much. I can't say specifically what I heard then.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did there come a time where you went to look for your brother?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, six or seven days later, I went to our parents' house where my brother lived with his wife and small child. It was a baby, three or four months old. I went there to look for him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And was he there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ANTUNOVIC
utterances.text: No. Later on I found out that he also left on the 1st of August in the direction of Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm prepared to conclude my examination for today at this point, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Biersay. Mr. Antunovic, your testimony for today comes to an end because we stop the hearing at 2.00. You will come back tomorrow at 9.00. You're still under oath, which means that you cannot discuss your testimony with anybody, and you cannot talk to any of the parties. You understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may leave the courtroom now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
